meta.blurb: The best general never has to fight. That is the strange claim of a book written about 2,500 years ago in China and credited to Sun Tzu. It says to win first, through planning, timing and knowing yourself and your rival.
meta.bible:
Sun Tzu: the thinker and general traditionally credited with the book; scholars disagree about who he was and when the text was finished. The Art of War: an ancient Chinese book of strategy in thirteen chapters, written about two and a half thousand years ago. China: the land of the Warring States. Wu and Yue: two old rival states of that region. Chapters in order: Laying Plans, Waging War, Attack by Stratagem, Tactical Dispositions, Energy, Weak Points and Strong, Maneuvering, Variation in Tactics, The Army on the March, Terrain, The Nine Situations, The Attack by Fire, The Use of Spies. Five factors: the way, heaven, earth, the commander, method. Five kinds of spies: local, inside, double, doomed, living. Key terms: Strategy, Stratagem, Commander, Deception, Siege, Morale, Terrain, Spies. Voice and tone: calm, clear and wise, like a teacher; the book is about avoiding war and winning wisely; fighting is treated factually and without gore; ideas are credited to the book and its tradition, never invented. King Helü of Wu: the ruler said to have hired Sun Tzu. Qi: the state Sun Tzu is said to have come from. Chu: a large state, rival of Wu. Sima Qian: a Chinese historian who wrote down the story of Sun Tzu about two thousand years ago.
 Cao Cao: a famous warlord of China about 1,800 years ago who wrote early notes on the book. Yinqueshan: a place in eastern China where bamboo strips with parts of the book were found in a tomb in 1972. Takeda Shingen: a sixteenth-century Japanese warlord who put the saying about wind, forest, fire and mountain on his banners. Amiot: Jean Joseph Marie Amiot, a missionary who made the first European translation, in French, in 1772. Yellow Emperor: a legendary ruler of early Chinese tradition. Shuairan: a snake from a famous mountain in the book's picture of a united army. Chapter order matches the bible above, with the story of the palace drill first. Chariots: war carts pulled by horses.

beats.scene: An ancient Chinese scholar writes on bamboo strips beside a lamp
beats.summary: Introduction: The Art of War is an ancient Chinese book of strategy, credited to Sun Tzu.

beats.scene: Small walled states and their banners are drawn on a large map
beats.summary: The book comes from an age when China was divided into rival states that were often at war.

beats.scene: A historian in a robe copies a life story onto a long scroll
beats.summary: A Chinese historian named Sima Qian wrote down the traditional story of Sun Tzu about two thousand years ago.

beats.scene: A traveller with a bundle of bamboo strips walks toward a southern palace
beats.summary: Sun Tzu travels to the state of Wu and shows his writings to King Helü.

beats.scene: A king points to a courtyard full of women in silk robes
beats.summary: King Helü asks Sun Tzu to show his method by training the women of the palace.

beats.scene: Two columns of women hold spears while two ladies stand at their heads
beats.summary: Sun Tzu forms the women into two companies and puts the king's two favourites at their head.

beats.scene: A drum stands on a stand while a calm man explains with his hands
beats.summary: Sun Tzu explains the drill commands clearly, again and again, and then beats the drum.

beats.scene: A stern general raises a hand as two ladies stand in the courtyard
beats.summary: When the women laugh a second time, Sun Tzu says the fault is now the officers', and the two leaders are put to death; the story says the king protested.

beats.scene: Rows of women march in perfect time as the king watches
beats.summary: With new leaders, the women drill perfectly, and Sun Tzu reports that the troops are ready.

beats.scene: A king sits in his palace while a new general studies a map
beats.summary: The king is grieved, but he sees Sun Tzu's skill, makes him a general, and the book is placed before the world.

beats.scene: A general stands before a large map spread across a table
beats.summary: Chapter 1, Laying Plans: Sun Tzu says war is vital to a country and must be studied with great care.

beats.scene: Five smooth stones lie in a row beside an old map
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu names five things to weigh before any war: the way, heaven, earth, the commander and method.

beats.scene: A king and his people stand together on a hillside at sunrise
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The first factor, the way, means that the people share their ruler's purpose.

beats.scene: Dark clouds gather over a camp as soldiers shiver in the cold
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The second factor, heaven, means weather, seasons and the time of day or year.

beats.scene: An army crosses a narrow mountain pass above a deep valley
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The third factor, earth, means distance, hills, open ground and narrow passes.

beats.scene: A calm commander gives an order while his officers listen closely
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The fourth factor, the commander, needs wisdom, honesty, kindness, courage and strictness.

beats.scene: Officers in neat ranks check boxes of supplies in a long camp
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The fifth factor, method, means organisation, clear ranks, rules and supplies.

beats.scene: An old general counts on his fingers beside five lit lamps
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu says every general has heard of the five factors, but only the one who really understands them will win.

beats.scene: Ministers gather in a quiet stone temple around a table of small markers
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Rulers made their calculations in a temple before a campaign; the one who counted most carefully won.

beats.scene: A king hands a general a staff of command while another man walks away
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu says a general who follows his advice should be kept in command, and one who does not should be dismissed.

beats.scene: Seven small flags stand in a row on a table beside a rolled scroll
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu proposes seven questions that compare two armies.

beats.scene: Two rulers sit on opposite sides of a table, one calm and one anxious
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The first two questions are which ruler is wiser and which general is abler.

beats.scene: A map shows high mountains on one side and an open plain
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The third and fourth questions ask who has the better weather and ground, and who keeps better discipline.

beats.scene: Two long rows of soldiers drill in the sun while officers watch
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The fifth and sixth questions ask which army is stronger and which has better trained officers and men.

beats.scene: A leader hands a reward to a kneeling soldier while another waits in line
beats.summary: Chapter 1: The seventh question asks which army is more consistent in giving rewards and punishments.

beats.scene: A general studies a table with many counting stones on one side
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu says many calculations lead to victory and few to defeat, and no calculation at all to certain defeat.

beats.scene: A smiling general stands behind a screen as the enemy looks away
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu says that all warfare is based on deception.

beats.scene: A strong soldier pretends to stumble while a weak one stands tall in armour
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu says to look weak when strong, and unready when ready.

beats.scene: A small basket of bright coins sits in a trap beside a quiet road
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu advises offering bait, causing disorder, and being ready when the enemy is strong.

beats.scene: A calm general hides a letter as an angry enemy captain shouts
beats.summary: Chapter 1: Sun Tzu lists ways to upset the enemy and says the secrets of victory cannot be known beforehand.

beats.scene: Rows of war chariots and thousands of soldiers wait on a wide plain
beats.summary: Chapter 2, Waging War: Sun Tzu begins with the size of an army, a thousand chariots and a hundred thousand soldiers.

beats.scene: Heavy bags of silver coins are carried out of a palace treasury
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu says an army in the field costs a huge sum every day, at home and at the front.

beats.scene: Broken spears and dull swords lie in the mud beside tired men
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu warns that a long war blunts weapons, dampens spirits and drains the strength of a state.

beats.scene: A neighbouring ruler watches a weak country from the top of a tower
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu says rival rulers take advantage of a weak, tired state, and no one can then save it.

beats.scene: A fast column of riders gallops ahead while a slow army lags behind
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu prefers a quick victory, even a clumsy one, to a long and clever campaign.

beats.scene: A thoughtful adviser shakes his head as a ruler calls for more taxes
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu says that only a person who understands the harm of war can understand how to use it well.

beats.scene: Soldiers load captured sacks of grain onto their own wagons
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu advises living off the enemy's land, because a single cartload taken there is worth twenty from home.

beats.scene: Poor farmers watch a long line of wagons pass their empty fields
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu explains that supplying a far-off army makes the people poor, and that prices rise wherever an army is.

beats.scene: Soldiers are honoured for capturing wagons and put flags on them
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu says to reward the first soldier who captures ten enemy chariots and to change their flags.

beats.scene: A kind officer gives bread to prisoners seated in a camp
beats.summary: Chapter 2: Sun Tzu says captured soldiers should be treated kindly, and that the aim of war is victory, not long campaigns.

beats.scene: Two walled cities stand untouched under a clear sky as an army turns back
beats.summary: Chapter 3, Attack by Stratagem: Sun Tzu says the best victory is to take a country whole, without fighting.

beats.scene: A small unit of soldiers walks calmly into a quiet town square
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says the same is true of armies, regiments and companies: it is better to capture them whole than to destroy them.

beats.scene: A neat set of wooden steps rises toward a council table at the top
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu ranks four ways to fight, and says the best is to spoil the enemy's plans.

beats.scene: A messenger leads two former friends away from a king's tent
beats.summary: Chapter 3: The second-best way is to break the enemy's alliances so that he stands alone.

beats.scene: A long line of soldiers faces another line across an open field
beats.summary: Chapter 3: The third way is to attack the enemy's army in the field, and the worst is to attack his walled cities.

beats.scene: Workers build tall wooden shields and wheeled towers outside a city wall
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says a siege takes months of preparation, with shelters, machines and earth ramps.

beats.scene: Soldiers swarm up ladders against a high city wall like ants
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says an impatient general sends his men swarming up the walls, and a third of them are lost while the city still stands.

beats.scene: A commander at a table receives the keys of a city from smiling officials
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says a skilled leader takes cities without a siege and ends a war without a long fight.

beats.scene: A calm commander looks at a map as his rested army sleeps nearby
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says that with his army whole, a skilled leader wins the contest without losing a single man.

beats.scene: Soldiers in different numbers stand around a circle drawn on the ground
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu gives rules for how to act when you have more, equal or fewer soldiers than the enemy.

beats.scene: A strong commander stands guard on a high wall with his arm raised
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says the commander is the support of the state: if he is complete, the state is strong.

beats.scene: A distant king shouts orders from his palace to a confused army
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu names three ways a ruler can bring trouble on his own army.

beats.scene: Soldiers argue in a camp as a rival messenger watches from the trees
beats.summary: Chapter 3: When an army is confused and doubtful, rival rulers come, and the army is beaten by its own side.

beats.scene: A commander counts five small flags laid out in a line on a table
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu gives five signs that show who will win.

beats.scene: Two travellers read a map: one holds a lantern and one stands in shadow
beats.summary: Chapter 3: Sun Tzu says that knowing yourself and your enemy means you need not fear a hundred battles.

beats.scene: A soldier builds a wall of shields in front of a quiet camp
beats.summary: Chapter 4, Tactical Dispositions: Sun Tzu says first make yourself impossible to beat, then wait for a chance.

beats.scene: A soldier hides in a deep hollow while another stands on a peak
beats.summary: Chapter 4: Sun Tzu says to defend when you are weak and attack when you are strong.

beats.scene: A quiet man lifts a feather while a crowd cheers a strong man
beats.summary: Chapter 4: Sun Tzu says the best winners win so easily that nobody praises them.

beats.scene: A general sits calmly in a tent while his soldiers rest before a battle
beats.summary: Chapter 4: Sun Tzu says a winning army wins first, then goes to battle, and a losing army does the opposite.

beats.scene: A heavy weight and a single grain sit on a scale
beats.summary: Chapter 4: Sun Tzu says a well-prepared army against an unprepared one is like a heavy weight against a single grain.

beats.scene: A general divides a crowd of soldiers into neat groups with coloured cords
beats.summary: Chapter 5, Energy: Sun Tzu says a large army is managed like a small one by dividing it into groups.

beats.scene: Drummers and flag-bearers on a hill direct a vast army below
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says that signals, drums, gongs and flags let a whole army move as one.

beats.scene: A bold front line meets a hidden group that appears from the side
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says an army can stand firm against any attack by using direct and indirect methods together.

beats.scene: A great wheel turns beside the sun, the moon and a changing season
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says indirect tactics are as endless as heaven and earth, and as unending as the seasons.

beats.scene: A musician plays a long flute while five coloured ribbons weave in the air
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says there are only five musical notes, yet their combinations are more than anyone can hear.

beats.scene: Five coloured paints and five dishes of food sit on a table
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu adds that there are only five colours and five tastes, yet they make more shades and flavours than can be tasted.

beats.scene: A calm commander turns a wheel while two columns circle each other
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says direct and indirect methods turn into each other like a circle with no end.

beats.scene: A falcon swoops from the sky onto a small bird in the grass
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu compares a perfectly timed attack to a falcon's strike and an energy that is released at once.

beats.scene: Noisy fighting soldiers move while an officer in the middle stays calm and orderly
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says that in the middle of confusion there must be no disorder, and false disorder needs perfect discipline.

beats.scene: A round stone rolls down a tall mountain while a square one stays still
beats.summary: Chapter 5: Sun Tzu says a skilled commander uses the combined energy of the army, like a round stone rolling down a steep mountain.

beats.scene: A rested army waits on a hill while a tired one hurries across
beats.summary: Chapter 6, Weak Points and Strong: Sun Tzu says to arrive first and make the enemy come to you.

beats.scene: A strong general moves a small chess-like piece while the enemy watches
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says the skilful fighter imposes his will on the enemy and does not let the enemy impose his on him.

beats.scene: A bowl of rice sits on one path while a gate closes another
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says an enemy can be drawn forward by a chance of profit, or held back by a threat of harm.

beats.scene: A comfortable enemy camp with full tables as a scout watches from a tree
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says to harass a rested enemy, starve one that is well fed, and force a quiet one to move.

beats.scene: A fast column marches toward a distant city while the enemy runs elsewhere
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says to appear where the enemy must hurry to defend, and to march quickly where you are not expected.

beats.scene: An army walks through an empty countryside under a calm sky
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says an army can march a long way without tiring if it passes through country where the enemy is not.

beats.scene: A hungry soldier tries to enter an unguarded door in a thick wall
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says you take what you attack if you attack where the enemy is not defended, and you hold what you defend if it cannot be attacked.

beats.scene: A shadow of a general slips past a lit camp without a sound
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu praises the divine art of subtlety and secrecy, which makes a general invisible and silent.

beats.scene: A fast scout runs ahead while the enemy gives chase and falls behind
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says an army can advance irresistibly by striking weak points and retreat safely by being quicker than the enemy.

beats.scene: A general draws lines on the ground while an enemy general stares in confusion
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says a general can force a fight by attacking a place the enemy must help, or avoid one by confusing him.

beats.scene: A general in plain clothes studies a camp from a hidden hill
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says that by finding out the enemy's plans and hiding our own, we can keep our forces together while he must divide his.

beats.scene: One large fist and ten small fingers face each other on a table
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says that a united army meeting a divided one fights many against few.

beats.scene: A hidden line of soldiers waits while the enemy scatters guards across many gates
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says the place of battle must stay secret, so the enemy prepares for many attacks and is weak at each.

beats.scene: A worried commander guards the front, the rear and both sides of a road
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says to strengthen the front is to weaken the rear, and that being weak in number comes from having to prepare against attack.

beats.scene: Two armies march toward one field, one by many roads
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says that knowing the time and place of battle lets us gather from far away, and that the larger army of Yue will not help it.

beats.scene: A scout pokes a sleeping camp with a stick and watches who stirs
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says to rouse the enemy, force him to show himself, and compare his army with your own.

beats.scene: A mist-like figure with no face walks through a battlefield
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says the highest skill is to be so hidden that even a clever spy can find nothing, and that people see tactics but not the strategy behind them.

beats.scene: A general looks at a fresh map while old maps lie in a pile
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says not to repeat the tactics that have won one victory, because the situations are endlessly different.

beats.scene: Water rushes down from a mountain and avoids a tall rock
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says military tactics are like water, which flows from high places to low, and an army should avoid strength and strike weakness.

beats.scene: A stream bends around different rocks while a boat follows its course
beats.summary: Chapter 6: Sun Tzu says water has no constant shape, and a general who changes with the enemy is called heaven-born; he adds the seasons and the moon.

beats.scene: A general in a tent receives a royal order, then leads soldiers out
beats.summary: Chapter 7, Maneuvering: Sun Tzu says a general gets his orders, gathers his army and blends it into harmony before he camps.

beats.scene: A long winding road and a short hidden path run toward the same hill
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says the hardest part of manoeuvring is to make the long way short, and to arrive first after setting out later.

beats.scene: A well-ordered army marches in step while a loud crowd stumbles behind
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says manoeuvring with a disciplined army is useful, but with an undisciplined crowd it is dangerous.

beats.scene: A fast small column pulls ahead while a heavy baggage train falls behind
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says that rushing a full army to seize an advantage may make it late, while sending a fast column means leaving its supplies behind.

beats.scene: Exhausted soldiers stumble along a night road with torches burning low
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu warns that a forced march wears out an army, with the strong in front, the weak behind, and only one in ten arriving after a very long march.

beats.scene: An empty supply wagon stands alone on a dusty road
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says an army without its baggage, food and supplies is lost.

beats.scene: A guide with a lantern points the way through marshes and pine forests
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says a general must know the country, with its mountains, forests, cliffs and swamps, and must use local guides.

beats.scene: A general nods slowly as his officers share out cloth, grain and land
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says to act only when there is a real gain, to decide by circumstances whether to gather or divide, and to share plunder and land among the soldiers.

beats.scene: A man in a long robe walks the wrong way on a bent road
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says the leader who first learns the way of the roundabout road wins, and this is the art of manoeuvring.

beats.scene: A drum and a gong sit beside folded flags in a quiet camp
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu quotes an old military book that says the voice cannot carry far in battle, so gongs, drums, banners and flags are used.

beats.scene: Banners show wind and a forest on a hillside above an army
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says an army should be swift as the wind and close and quiet as a forest.

beats.scene: Banners show fire and a mountain above a burning field
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says to be fierce as fire when raiding and unmoving as a mountain when holding.

beats.scene: A dark night above a camp as lightning strikes in the distance
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says plans should be dark and unseen as night, and that when you move you should strike like a thunderbolt.

beats.scene: A hundred soldiers move together as if tied by invisible ribbons
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says gongs, drums and flags make the army one body, so the brave cannot advance alone and the cowardly cannot retreat alone.

beats.scene: A burning torch stands in a dark camp beside a flag
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says to use many fires and drums at night, and flags by day, to guide the army's eyes and ears.

beats.scene: A soldier stands blank-faced while a general sits worried at a tent
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says a whole army can be robbed of its spirit, and a general of his presence of mind.

beats.scene: A rising sun, a midday sun and a setting sun above one marching army
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says a soldier's spirit is keenest in the morning, flags by noon, and by evening he thinks only of rest; a clever general strikes when it is low.

beats.scene: A calm army sits in order while the other army shouts and runs
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says that being disciplined and calm while the enemy is disordered is the art of mastering self-control, and to be near while he is far and rested while he is tired.

beats.scene: A banner stands perfectly straight in front of a still army on a hill
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu gives maxims on what not to do, such as do not attack troops in good order, do not follow a pretended flight, and do not take bait.

beats.scene: A small gap opens in a ring of soldiers around a tired enemy camp
beats.summary: Chapter 7: Sun Tzu says to leave a way out when you surround an army, and not to press a desperate enemy too hard.

beats.scene: A general at a crossroads picks one small path beside an empty road
beats.summary: Chapter 8, Variation in Tactics: Sun Tzu says that in difficult country you do not camp, at crossroads you join your friends, and in dangerous places you do not linger.

beats.scene: Five signposts point to a road, an army, a town, a post, a letter
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu lists things not to do: roads not to follow, armies not to attack, towns not to besiege, places not to contest, orders not to obey.

beats.scene: A student reads a map while a teacher points to a bend
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu says a general who understands variation knows how to use his troops, and one who does not will fail to use his knowledge of the ground.

beats.scene: A scale holds a coin on one side and a small stone
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu says a wise leader always weighs both the advantages and the disadvantages of a plan.

beats.scene: A worried ruler counts silver while his rival's courier hurries past
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu says a rival state can be weakened by harming it, troubling it and tempting it to hurry to a given place.

beats.scene: A guard on a wall looks out at a quiet horizon
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu says to rely not on the enemy not coming, but on our own readiness to receive him.

beats.scene: A reckless soldier runs forward while a trembling one hides behind a rock
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu lists the first two of five faults that can ruin a general: recklessness, which leads to being killed, and cowardice, which leads to being captured.

beats.scene: A man tears up a letter while another pats his own chest in pride
beats.summary: Chapter 8: The other three faults are a hasty temper, a delicate sense of honour, and too much concern for his men.

beats.scene: Five empty armour stands cast long shadows across a battlefield
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Sun Tzu says these five faults ruin the conduct of war, and when an army is beaten, the cause will be found among them.

beats.scene: A traveller stops at a signpost where several roads meet
beats.summary: Chapter 8: Taken together, the chapter says a rule is a tool, and a good general knows when to set it aside.

beats.scene: An army camps on a sunny hillside above a valley
beats.summary: Chapter 9, The Army on the March: Sun Tzu says that in the mountains an army should stay near valleys, camp high and face the sun, and not climb to fight.

beats.scene: Soldiers wade through a river while a rival army waits on the far bank
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says to move far from a river after crossing it, and to strike an enemy who is crossing when half of his army is across.

beats.scene: Boats are tied up at a bank higher than the enemy's, facing the sun
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says not to go upstream to meet an enemy, and to keep your boats higher than the enemy's, facing the sun.

beats.scene: Soldiers cross a salt marsh quickly with tall grass around them
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says to cross salt marshes quickly, and if forced to fight there, to stay near water and grass with trees behind you.

beats.scene: An army sits on open dry land with a low hill rising behind it
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that on dry, level country you should take a place where you can move easily, with rising ground behind you.

beats.scene: A legendary emperor in a gold robe stands with four defeated rulers behind him
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that these four useful lessons helped the legendary Yellow Emperor defeat four rival rulers.

beats.scene: Soldiers sleep on dry ground in a camp full of sunlight
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says armies prefer high ground to low and sunny to dark, and that a camp on firm ground is free of disease.

beats.scene: A slope faces the sun as a general points to a tent site
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that when you come to a hill or a bank, you should occupy the sunny side with the slope at your right rear.

beats.scene: A swollen brown river with foam as soldiers wait on the bank
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that when heavy rain upstream makes a river swollen and foamy, you must wait until it goes down.

beats.scene: Cliffs, deep hollows, thorn thickets and a muddy swamp lie around a quiet road
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says to leave quickly any place with steep cliffs, deep hollows, thickets or swamps, and to lure the enemy into such places.

beats.scene: A scout looks at a pond, reeds and thick bushes near a camp
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says to search hills, ponds with tall grass, reedy hollows and thick woods near your camp, because hidden men or spies may be there.

beats.scene: A silent enemy camp sits on a rocky height while a scout watches
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that a quiet enemy who is close is relying on a strong position, and one who stays far away and provokes a fight wants you to advance.

beats.scene: Trees move on a hillside while straw dummies stand in the grass
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that movement among trees shows an enemy is coming, and that screens in thick grass mean he wants to make you suspicious.

beats.scene: Birds rise suddenly from a quiet wood as a scout looks up
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that birds rising suddenly show an ambush, and startled animals show a surprise attack.

beats.scene: A tall column of dust rises from a road beside a low cloud
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that a high, narrow dust column means chariots coming, and a low, wide cloud means foot soldiers.

beats.scene: A messenger arrives with a bow while soldiers behind him check their spears
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says humble words with more preparations show that the enemy will attack, and violent words with a rush forward show that he will retreat.

beats.scene: Light chariots take up positions on the wings of an army
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that light chariots coming first on the flanks show the enemy is forming for battle, and that peace proposals with no oath suggest a plot.

beats.scene: Hungry soldiers lean on their spears beside a dry well
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that signs such as leaning on spears, drinking first at the well, birds on an empty camp, and shouting at night show hunger, thirst, emptiness and fear.

beats.scene: A large army sits uselessly while a smaller united army calmly watches it
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that numbers alone do not give victory, and a commander who is careless and underestimates his enemy will be taken.

beats.scene: A commander gives a bowl of food to a soldier and reads the rules
beats.summary: Chapter 9: Sun Tzu says that soldiers punished before they are attached will not obey, and that a commander who is trusting yet firm gains the men's loyalty.

beats.scene: Six different landscapes are drawn side by side on one long map
beats.summary: Chapter 10, Terrain: Sun Tzu names six kinds of ground, and begins with accessible ground, where you should take the high sunny places and guard your supplies first.

beats.scene: A narrow path leads into a valley as a tired army turns back
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says entangling ground is easy to enter and hard to leave, and temporising ground is where neither side gains by moving first.

beats.scene: A small army holds a narrow mountain pass with a wall of shields
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says that in narrow passes you should occupy them first and fill them with a strong force.

beats.scene: A sunny peak stands high above a long dusty road leading far away
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says to take the sunny side of precipitous heights first, and that when the enemy is far away it is hard to provoke a battle.

beats.scene: A thoughtful general studies hills, rivers and distances on a small table map
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says the shape of the land is a soldier's best ally, but the test of a great general is to estimate the enemy, the dangers and the distances.

beats.scene: Six broken pieces of armour lie in a line on a table
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu names six kinds of calamity that an army can meet, which come not from nature but from the general's faults.

beats.scene: Soldiers run away from a huge army while strong men refuse an officer's order
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Flight happens when a small army attacks a much larger one, insubordination when soldiers are strong and officers weak, and collapse when officers are strong and soldiers weak.

beats.scene: Angry officers rush off alone while a general looks lost in a muddled camp
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Ruin comes when angry officers fight on their own, disorganisation when a weak general gives unclear orders, and rout when he sends weak troops against strong ones.

beats.scene: A commander in plain armour walks away from honour toward his men
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says that a general who advances without seeking fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, thinking only of his country, is the jewel of the kingdom.

beats.scene: A leader gives bread to a young soldier and corrects a careless one
beats.summary: Chapter 10: Sun Tzu says a general who treats his men like his own children will be followed anywhere, but kindness without firmness makes them useless like spoiled children.

beats.scene: Nine small flags with different signs stand around a map
beats.summary: Chapter 11, The Nine Situations: Sun Tzu names nine kinds of ground, and says that dispersive ground is fought in your own land where soldiers want to run home.

beats.scene: An army marches only a little way into enemy country, then keeps moving
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that facile ground is shallow enemy country, where an army should not stop, and that contentious ground is a place both sides want.

beats.scene: Many roads cross in open country where messengers from several states meet
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that on open ground you should not block the enemy, and at crossroads you should join hands with your allies.

beats.scene: An army has gone deep into enemy country with castles left behind it
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that on serious ground you should gather supplies from the land, and on difficult ground you should keep going.

beats.scene: A narrow gorge entrance and a cliff wall trap a small band of soldiers
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says on hemmed-in ground you should use stratagem, and on desperate ground, where only fighting saves you, you must fight at once.

beats.scene: Two groups of soldiers shout across a river but cannot meet
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that skilful commanders of old made the enemy unable to join his front and rear, and unable to help his large and small parts.

beats.scene: A general quietly takes a treasured chest from a rich enemy house
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that to deal with a large, orderly enemy, you should begin by seizing something he holds dear.

beats.scene: Fast riders cross open ground in the early morning mist
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that speed is the essence of war, and that you should take advantage of the enemy's unreadiness and travel by unexpected routes.

beats.scene: An army marches deep into a rich country and gathers grain from large fields
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that the deeper an invading army goes, the more united it becomes, and it should live off fertile land and take care of its men.

beats.scene: A line of soldiers walks away from a burning ruin into a dark pass
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that a commander should keep the army moving and that his plans should be impossible to see through.

beats.scene: Soldiers stand with their backs to a cliff and a river, looking determined
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that soldiers put where there is no escape will prefer death to flight, and will use their uttermost strength.

beats.scene: A frightened soldier steadies himself and grips a spear tightly
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says soldiers in desperate straits lose their fear and, with no help for it, will fight hard.

beats.scene: A band of soldiers stays alert in the dark without being told to
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says such an army needs no commands, stays alert and faithful, and should be freed from omens and superstition.

beats.scene: Soldiers with small bundles of silver weep quietly in a lamplit tent
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says soldiers do not hate wealth or long life, but before a battle they may weep, and once brought to bay they will show great courage.

beats.scene: A long snake coils on a high mountain and raises its head and tail
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu compares a skilful army to the shuairan snake, which answers every blow at its head, tail or middle.

beats.scene: Two boats ride the same storm while rival crews help each other
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says that men of Wu and Yue, though enemies, helped each other like the left hand and the right when crossing a river in a storm.

beats.scene: Horses are tied and wagon wheels buried, but soldiers look uneasy
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says it is not enough to tie horses and bury wheels, and that the way to manage an army is to give all one standard of courage.

beats.scene: A general leads a long line of men by the hand through dark hills
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says the skilful general leads his army as if leading one man by the hand, and must be calm, fair and able to keep his plans secret.

beats.scene: A burning boat floats down a river behind soldiers on the far bank
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says a leader of an army acts like one who climbs up a height and kicks away the ladder, and burns his boats and breaks his cooking pots.

beats.scene: A shy maiden stands at a door and a swift hare runs through it
beats.summary: Chapter 11: Sun Tzu says to be as shy as a maiden until the enemy gives an opening, and then as swift as a running hare.

beats.scene: Five small fires burn at five targets in an enemy camp at night
beats.summary: Chapter 12, The Attack by Fire: Sun Tzu names five ways to attack with fire: burning soldiers, stores, baggage trains, arsenals and dropping fire.

beats.scene: Dry grass, bundles of straw and a torch are stacked beside a hut
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says that to carry out a fire attack you need the means ready, and the material for raising a fire must always be at hand.

beats.scene: A dry field beneath a night sky with a group of stars shining
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says there is a right season for fire, when the weather is dry, and special days when the moon is in four star groups that mean wind.

beats.scene: A flame leaps up in an enemy camp as soldiers outside wait with weapons
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says to be ready for five developments, such as attacking from outside when the fire breaks out inside.

beats.scene: A line of fire races across dry grass with a strong wind behind it
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says to attack when the flames are at their height if it can be done, and otherwise to stay put; and always be on the side the wind blows from.

beats.scene: A flag blows strongly in the daytime and hangs limply at night
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says a wind that rises in the day lasts long and a night breeze soon falls, and every army must know the stars and watch for the right days.

beats.scene: A stream is directed across a road beside a blazing hut
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says those who use fire to help an attack show intelligence, those who use water gain strength, but water cannot rob the enemy of everything.

beats.scene: A commander in a plain tent writes careful notes on a scroll
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says that winning battles without a spirit of enterprise leads to waste of time, and that the wise ruler plans ahead and the good general builds up his resources.

beats.scene: A calm general rests his chin on his hand as an officer points
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says to move only if you see an advantage, to use troops only if there is something to gain, and to fight only if the position is critical.

beats.scene: An angry ruler tears up a letter while a calm adviser waits beside him
beats.summary: Chapter 12: Sun Tzu says a ruler must not go to war out of anger, because a destroyed kingdom cannot come back and the dead cannot live again.

beats.scene: Thousands of soldiers march along a road while farmers stop work to watch
beats.summary: Chapter 13, The Use of Spies: Sun Tzu says a large army on a long march costs the people dearly, with a thousand pieces of silver a day and many families unable to work.

beats.scene: Two armies face each other across a river, with tents in the snow
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says armies may face one another for years for a victory decided in a day, and that it is inhuman to stay ignorant of the enemy to save a little money.

beats.scene: A king with empty hands stands beside a wise general holding a rolled message
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says that a ruler who will not pay for information is no leader of men, and that what lets a wise ruler conquer is foreknowledge.

beats.scene: A general in a lamplit tent listens to a quiet traveller in a hood
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says foreknowledge cannot come from spirits, from experience or from calculation, but only from people who know the enemy's situation.

beats.scene: Five figures in plain clothes stand in a row, each holding a different lantern
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu names five kinds of spies: local, inside, double, doomed and living; when all five are at work, no one can discover the system.

beats.scene: A farmer and an official in robes each pass a whisper to a stranger
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says local spies are people living in the enemy's district, and inside spies are the enemy's own officials.

beats.scene: A spy in a double cloak crosses a bridge between two camps
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says that double spies are enemy spies turned to our side, doomed spies carry false news, and living spies bring back reports.

beats.scene: A general quietly hands a heavy purse to a hooded man
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says no one in the army is closer to the general than the spies, none should be better rewarded, and none must be handled with greater secrecy.

beats.scene: A general reads a message by candlelight and compares it with another
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says to be subtle and use spies for every kind of business, and that a leaked secret is a grave fault, so a spy must be handled with the strictest care.

beats.scene: A gold thread connects a map of the enemy to a single quiet room
beats.summary: Chapter 13: Sun Tzu says the double spy is the most important, because from him we find the local and inside spies, and that the old rulers of dynasties used men who had served the enemy.

beats.scene: A scholar ties the last bamboo strip to a long roll by lamplight
beats.summary: The thirteen chapters end: the book began with a warning about war and ends with a plain lesson about knowing.

beats.scene: Scribes copy rolls of text beside an old general writing notes
beats.summary: The book was copied by hand for centuries, and a famous warlord named Cao Cao wrote early notes on it about 1,800 years ago.

beats.scene: An archaeologist carefully lifts old bamboo strips from a tomb
beats.summary: In 1972, workers found bamboo strips with the text of the book in a tomb at Yinqueshan, which was about two thousand years old.

beats.scene: A warlord in armour stands before a great banner with four lines of characters
beats.summary: The book reached Japan, where the sixteenth-century warlord Takeda Shingen put its saying about wind, forest, fire and mountain on his banners.

beats.scene: A missionary in black robes writes at a desk with a Chinese book open
beats.summary: In 1772, a Jesuit missionary named Amiot published the first European translation, in French, and it was later translated into many other languages.

beats.scene: A manager, a chess player, a lawyer and a runner read one book
beats.summary: Today the book is read not only by soldiers, but also by business leaders, sports coaches, lawyers and others who must compete or negotiate.

beats.scene: A reader frowns at a screen of famous quotations, some crossed out
beats.summary: Many popular lines said to be by Sun Tzu cannot be found in the book, so a careful reader should check them.

beats.scene: An old soldier sets down a sword and looks at green growing grain
beats.summary: The book comes from a world of chariots and walls, so it should be read with judgement, but it is also humane: it praises restraint, kindness to prisoners and an escape for a beaten enemy.

beats.scene: A calm figure walks away from a quarrel, leaving two people arguing
beats.summary: The best victory is the one that never needs a fight, and this lesson applies to everyday disputes, talks and plans.

beats.scene: A modern reader opens an old book at a desk by a window
beats.summary: Conclusion: The Art of War is still read today, and its main lesson is that wisdom, preparation and restraint beat force.

B1B2: The Art of War is one of the oldest books about strategy in the world. It is credited to Sun Tzu, a Chinese thinker who lived about two and a half thousand years ago.
In Sun Tzu's day, China was divided into many rival states, and their rulers fought one another again and again. A ruler who lost a war could lose his whole country.
Most of what we know about Sun Tzu comes from the historian Sima Qian, who lived about two thousand years ago. He says that Sun Tzu came from the state of Qi.
The story says that Sun Tzu travelled to the southern state of Wu. There he showed his thirteen chapters on war to King Helü.
King Helü said that the thirteen chapters were very good, but he wanted to see the ideas used. He asked Sun Tzu to train some of the women of his palace as soldiers.
The story says that there were about one hundred and eighty women. Sun Tzu divided them into two groups and made the king's two favourite ladies the leaders.
Sun Tzu explained the orders again and again, so that every woman knew what turn right, turn left and turn back meant. Then he beat the drum to begin the drill.
Sun Tzu said that unclear orders are the general's fault, so he explained them again. When the women laughed a second time, he said the officers were at fault, and the two leaders were put to death.
Two new leaders were chosen, and the drill began again. This time the women turned, marched and knelt exactly as they were told, and nobody dared to make a sound.
The king was upset, and he told Sun Tzu to go back to his tent. Even so, he saw that Sun Tzu knew how to lead an army, and he made him a general.
Sun Tzu begins by saying that war is a matter of life and death for a country. It can lead to safety or to ruin, so it must never be entered carelessly.
Sun Tzu names five things that decide a war: the way, heaven, earth, the commander and method. A wise leader must study all five carefully before he decides anything at all.
The way means that the people and their ruler share the same goal. When they do, the people will follow him through danger without fear.
Heaven means everything that time and weather bring: day and night, heat and cold, and the changing seasons. A good leader chooses the right time to move his army.
Earth means the shape of the land, which may be near or far, open or narrow, safe or dangerous. Whoever knows the ground well fights with a great advantage.
The commander must have five qualities: wisdom, honesty, kindness, courage and strictness. Without them, even the best plan will fail in his hands.
Method is the way an army is organised, with clear ranks, firm rules and a steady supply of food. A well-run army is much harder to defeat than a muddled one.
Sun Tzu says that every general has heard of these five factors. The one who truly understands them will win, and the one who does not will fail.
In old China, a ruler made his plans in the family temple before he sent out an army. Sun Tzu says that the general who counts the most carefully there is the one who wins in the field.
Sun Tzu is sure that his advice is good. He tells the king that a general who follows it will win and should be kept, but one who ignores it should be sent away.
To compare two sides, Sun Tzu asks seven questions. He says that the answers will show who is likely to win and who is likely to lose.
The first question is which ruler has the trust of his people. The second is which general has more skill, because a skilful general can win even with a poor army.
The third question is which side has the better weather and ground. The fourth is which army keeps its rules more strictly, because a disciplined army is a strong one.
The fifth question is which army is stronger in numbers and weapons. The sixth is on which side the officers and soldiers are better trained.
The seventh question is which side is more fair and steady in giving rewards and punishments. Soldiers fight best when they know that good work is always rewarded.
Sun Tzu says that a leader who makes many calculations is likely to win, and one who makes few is likely to lose. He asks what will happen to the leader who makes no calculations at all.
Sun Tzu says that all warfare is based on deception. A skilled leader hides the truth about his own side and makes the enemy believe something false.
When you are strong, you should look weak, and when you are ready, you should look unprepared. When you are near, seem far away, and when you are far, seem near.
Offer the enemy a small prize so that he walks into a trap, and cause him trouble if he is already disorganised. If he is strong, be ready for him, and if he is stronger than you, avoid him.
If the enemy is easily angered, annoy him, and if he is proud, let him think you are weak. If he is resting, give him no peace, and if his men are united, find a way to divide them.
In the chapter on waging war, Sun Tzu pictures a large army. It has a thousand fast chariots, a thousand heavy ones and a hundred thousand soldiers.
Sun Tzu says that the cost of such an army is enormous, with a thousand pieces of silver spent every day. Money is needed at home and at the front, for food, glue, paint and everything between.
When a war lasts a long time, weapons grow dull and the soldiers lose their spirit. Laying siege to a walled city drains the strength of an army even more.
When the country's money is gone and its army is tired, other rulers will take advantage. Even the wisest adviser then cannot save the state from the trouble it has made for itself.
Sun Tzu says that a quick, plain victory is better than a long and clever one. Speed saves money, lives and the strength of the army.
Sun Tzu says that only the person who understands the harm of war can really know how to use war well. A wise ruler does not call up soldiers twice or load supply wagons three times.
Sun Tzu advises an army to feed itself from the enemy's land. One cartload of food taken from the enemy, he says, is worth twenty cartloads carried from home.
Carrying supplies over long distances makes the people poor. Near an army, prices go up, and this drains the money of ordinary families.
When chariots are captured, Sun Tzu says, the man who took the first one should be rewarded. The enemy's flags are then replaced with your own, and the chariots are used by your army.
Sun Tzu says that captured soldiers should be treated well and, if possible, taken into your own army. He ends the chapter by saying that the aim of war is victory, not a long campaign.
In his chapter on attack by stratagem, Sun Tzu says that the best result is to take a country whole and unharmed. To win a hundred battles is good, but to win without fighting at all is better still.
Sun Tzu says that the same is true at every size. It is better to capture an army, a regiment or a small company whole than to destroy it.
Sun Tzu lists four ways to fight, from best to worst. The very best way is to spoil the enemy's plans before he can use them.
The next best way is to break the enemy's friendships with other states. When he has no allies, he is much weaker and easier to beat.
The third way is to attack the enemy's army in the field. The worst way of all is to attack his walled cities, which Sun Tzu says should be done only when there is no choice.
Preparing the shelters and machines for a siege takes three whole months. Piling up earth ramps against the walls takes three months more.
Sun Tzu says that a general who cannot control his anger sends his soldiers to swarm up the walls like ants. He may lose a third of them, and the city is still standing.
A skilled leader makes the enemy give up without a siege and ends a war without a long campaign. His victory is so quiet that few people even notice it.
Because the skilled leader keeps his army whole, he can compete for the leadership of the whole empire. In this way, his victory is complete without losing a single man.
Sun Tzu explains what to do according to numbers. With ten times the enemy's strength, surround him, and with five times, attack, but if you are weaker, you should avoid him.
Sun Tzu says that the commander is the wall that protects the state. If he is skilled in every way, the state will be strong, but if he has weaknesses, it will be weak.
Sun Tzu names three ways a ruler can harm his army. He may order it forward or back without knowing the facts, run it like a royal court, or give posts to unfit men.
When the army is restless and full of doubt, other rulers will see their chance and attack. In this way, the army's own ruler has brought confusion into its ranks and thrown away the victory.
Sun Tzu lists five signs of victory, such as knowing when to fight and when not to fight. The winner also has an army that is united and a ruler who does not interfere.
Sun Tzu gives his best-known advice: know your enemy and know yourself. If you know both, you need not fear a hundred battles, but if you know neither, you will lose every time.
In the chapter on tactical dispositions, Sun Tzu says that a good commander first makes himself impossible to defeat. Then he waits for the moment when the enemy can be beaten.

Sun Tzu says that a leader should defend when he lacks strength and attack when he has plenty. A good defender hides like someone deep underground, and a good attacker strikes like lightning from the sky.
Sun Tzu says that seeing a victory everyone can see is no great skill. Lifting a feather is no sign of strength, and seeing the sun and moon is no sign of sharp eyes.
The winning army wins first and goes to battle afterwards. The losing army goes to battle first and only then hopes to find a way to win.

Sun Tzu says that a ready army set against an unready one is like a heavy weight set against a single grain. The ready army, he adds, moves like a flood of water that has been held back and then let go.
In the chapter on energy, Sun Tzu says that managing a large army is the same as managing a small one. The secret is to divide it into groups, each with its own leader.
To fight a large army as if it were one man, you need clear signals. Drums and gongs are used where soldiers cannot see, and flags are used where they cannot hear.
To make the whole army able to meet any attack, Sun Tzu uses two ideas, the direct and the indirect. The direct force meets the enemy, and the indirect force surprises him.
Sun Tzu says that indirect tactics are endless, like heaven and earth. They end only to begin again, as the sun and moon rise and set and the seasons come and go.
There are only five musical notes, Sun Tzu says. Yet when they are combined, they make more tunes than anyone could ever hear.
In the same way, he says, there are only five basic colours and five basic tastes. Yet in combination, they make more shades and flavours than anyone could ever see or taste.
There are really only two methods in battle, the direct and the indirect, but they lead to each other in endless ways. It is like a circle that has no beginning and no end.

Sun Tzu says that a perfect attack is like the swoop of a falcon, which strikes its victim at just the right moment. Energy is like a bow that is slowly drawn, and decision is like the release of the string.
In the middle of noise and confusion, Sun Tzu says, there must be no real disorder. Pretending to be in disorder needs perfect discipline, and pretending to be weak needs real strength.
A skilled general looks for victory in the energy of the whole army, not in single soldiers. He is like a man who rolls round stones down a mountain, where a square stone would stay still.
In his chapter on weak points and strong, Sun Tzu says that the leader who arrives first on the battlefield waits at ease. The one who arrives later must hurry, and he comes already tired.
A skilful fighter forces his will on the enemy, and he never lets the enemy force his will on him. He decides where and when the fight will take place.
By offering the enemy an advantage, you can make him come closer. By threatening harm, you can make it impossible for him to approach.
If the enemy is resting, Sun Tzu says to harass him, and if his food is plentiful, to cut it off. If he is camped quietly, force him to move.
Sun Tzu says to show yourself at places the enemy must rush to defend. Then march quickly to places where he does not expect you.
An army can march a very long way without being tired, Sun Tzu says, if it goes through country where the enemy is not. A road with no enemy on it is an easy road.
You will be sure to take what you attack if you attack a place that is undefended. You will be sure to keep what you defend if the enemy cannot attack it.
Sun Tzu calls subtlety and secrecy a divine art. Through them, he says, a general becomes invisible and silent, and the enemy's fate is in his hands.
An army that makes for the enemy's weak points cannot be stopped as it advances. If it is quicker than the enemy, it can retreat safely.
If you want a battle, attack a place that the enemy must rescue, even if he is behind high walls. If you do not want one, you can stop it by puzzling him with something odd.
If we learn the enemy's plans while hiding our own, we can keep our army together. The enemy, who cannot see us, must divide his forces to guard against us.
When we are united and the enemy is split into parts, we meet each part with our whole army. In this way, we are many and he is few.
The place we mean to fight must be kept secret. Then the enemy has to prepare against attacks in many places, and he has only a few men at each one.

If the enemy guards his front, he weakens his rear, and if he guards his rear, he weakens his front. Weakness in numbers comes from having to prepare against attacks, and strength comes from forcing the enemy to prepare against us.
If we know the time and place of the battle, we can gather our forces from far away. Sun Tzu says that even though Yue has more soldiers than Wu, this will not give Yue the victory.

Sun Tzu says to rouse the enemy to learn how he acts, and to make him show himself so we can see his weak spots. We should compare his army with ours to see where we are strong and where we are short.
The highest skill in making plans is to hide them. Then even the cleverest spy cannot find out anything, and the enemy cannot make a plan against you.
Do not repeat the tactics which have won you one victory, Sun Tzu says. Let your methods change as the situation changes, for the situations are endless.
Sun Tzu compares military tactics to water, which flows from high places down to low ones. In the same way, an army should avoid what is strong and strike what is weak.
As water has no fixed shape, there are no fixed rules in war. A general who changes his plans to fit his enemy may be called heaven-born, like the seasons and the moon.
In the chapter on manoeuvring, Sun Tzu says that a general receives his orders from the ruler. He then gathers the army and makes it work together before he camps.
Sun Tzu says that the hardest part of manoeuvring is to take a long and winding road and make it work as a short one. A clever general may start after the enemy and still get there first.
Manoeuvring with an army can be to your advantage. But manoeuvring with an undisciplined crowd is very dangerous.
If you march a full army fast to seize an advantage, you will probably be too late. If you send a light column instead, you will have to leave the baggage and supplies behind.
Sun Tzu warns that a forced march without rest is dangerous. The strong arrive first and the weak fall behind, and after a very long march only about one in ten may arrive.
Sun Tzu says that an army without its baggage train is lost. It is also lost without food, and lost without a safe place to keep its supplies.
We should not lead an army on a march unless we know the land, with its mountains, forests, cliffs and swamps. A general should use local guides who know the country.
Sun Tzu says to move only when there is something real to gain. When you take plunder, share it among the men, and think carefully before every move.
Sun Tzu says that the leader who first learns the trick of the roundabout road will win. This, he says, is the real art of manoeuvring an army.
An old military book says that on the battlefield the voice does not carry far, so gongs and drums are used. Ordinary things cannot be seen clearly, so banners and flags are used instead.
Sun Tzu describes how an army should behave in a short list of images. It should be as swift as the wind, and as close and silent as a forest.
In raiding and plundering, be like fire, Sun Tzu says. When holding still, be like a mountain that cannot be moved.
Let your plans be dark and hidden like the night, Sun Tzu says. When you move, fall on the enemy like a thunderbolt.
Gongs, drums and flags keep every eye and ear of the army on one point. The army then moves as one body, so the brave cannot rush ahead and the fearful cannot run away alone.
In night fighting, he says, an army should use many fires and drums. In daytime fighting, an army should use many flags and banners.
A whole army may be robbed of its spirit, and a general may be robbed of his calm. When these are lost, the battle is half lost, too.
A soldier's spirit is sharpest in the morning and has started to fade by noon. By evening, his mind is on going back to camp, so a clever general attacks him then.
Be disciplined and calm, and wait for the enemy to fall into disorder. Be near the goal while he is far, rested while he is tired, and well fed while he is hungry.
Do not attack troops whose banners are in perfect order, and do not follow an enemy who pretends to run away. Do not attack soldiers who are in high spirits, and do not take the enemy's bait.
When you surround an army, leave it a way out. Do not press a desperate enemy too hard, because he will fight with the courage of despair.

In the chapter on variation in tactics, Sun Tzu gives short rules for different ground. Do not camp in difficult country, join your allies at crossroads, and do not linger in lonely, dangerous places.

There are roads which must not be followed, armies which must not be attacked and towns which must not be besieged. There are also positions which must not be contested and orders from the ruler which must not be obeyed.
A general who really understands variation knows how to handle his troops. One who does not may know the land well, but he will not be able to use that knowledge.
Sun Tzu says that a wise leader always weighs both the advantages and the disadvantages of a plan. By doing this, he can find a way out of trouble and keep a good plan from turning into a mistake.
Sun Tzu says that rival rulers can be reduced by harming them and kept constantly busy. They can also be tempted with rich prizes, so that they rush to wherever we want.
Sun Tzu says that we should not rely on the enemy not coming. We should rely on being ready for him, and on making our position too strong to attack.
Sun Tzu lists five faults that can ruin a general. The first is recklessness, which leads to destruction, and the second is cowardice, which leads to being captured.
The other three faults are a hasty temper, a pride that is easily hurt, and too much worry about one's men. A clever enemy can use each of these against the general.
Sun Tzu says that these five faults are ruinous to the conduct of war. When an army is beaten and its general is killed, the cause will be found among them.
Taken together, these lessons say that rules are tools. A good leader knows the rules well, and he also knows when a rule should be put aside.
In the chapter on the army on the march, Sun Tzu gives advice for mountains. Stay close to valleys, camp on high ground that faces the sun, and do not climb up to fight.
After crossing a river, get well away from it. If an enemy is crossing, do not meet him in the water, but wait until half his army is across and then attack.
Do not go up the river to meet the enemy, Sun Tzu says. If you want to fight, stay away from the river he must cross, and tie your boats higher up than his.
In salt marshes, the only thing to do is to get through them quickly and not stay. If you have to fight there, stay near water and grass, with a clump of trees behind you.
On dry, level ground, take up a position where you can move easily. Keep rising ground on your right and behind you, so that danger is in front and safety is behind.
Sun Tzu says that these four kinds of knowledge helped the Yellow Emperor, a legendary ruler, to defeat four other rulers. Tradition remembers him as one of the great figures of the Chinese past.
All armies prefer high ground to low, and sunny places to dark ones. If the commander cares for his men and camps on hard, dry ground, the army will be free from sickness.
When you come to a hill or a bank, take the sunny side with the slope on your right and behind you. In this way, you help your soldiers and use the land well.
If heavy rain upstream makes a river rise and fill with foam, do not try to cross it. You must wait patiently until the water has gone down again.
Sun Tzu says that cliffs with torrents, deep hollows, thickets and swamps should be left quickly and not approached. We should keep away from them and let the enemy go near them.
Near your camp, there may be hills, ponds with tall grass, hollows full of reeds or thick woods. Search them carefully, because enemy soldiers or spies may be hiding there.
When the enemy is close but quiet, he is relying on the strength of his position. When he stays far away and tries to start a fight, he wants you to come to him.
If the trees of a forest are moving, the enemy is probably advancing. If you see many screens in the thick grass, he is trying to make you suspicious.
The sudden rising of birds is a sign that men are hiding below. Startled animals running out of cover show that a sudden attack is coming.
A high, narrow column of dust shows that chariots are advancing. A low and wide cloud of dust shows that infantry soldiers are coming.
If the enemy speaks humbly but makes more preparations, he is about to advance. If he speaks violently and drives forward as if to attack, he may be about to retreat.
When the light chariots come out first and take their places on the wings, the enemy is getting ready for battle. Peace offers without a solemn promise often hide a plot.
Soldiers who lean on their spears are faint from hunger, and men who drink first at the well are thirsty. Birds on a camp mean it is empty, and shouting at night means the men are afraid.
Sun Tzu says that numbers alone do not give victory. A general who takes no thought and despises the enemy will be captured, but one who watches the enemy will win.
If soldiers are punished before they are loyal, they will not obey. If a commander is kind to his men but always makes sure that his orders are followed, both sides gain.
In the chapter on terrain, Sun Tzu names six kinds of ground. On open ground that both sides can reach easily, take the high, sunny places first and keep your supply roads safe.
Entangling ground is easy to enter but hard to leave. On temporising ground, neither side gains by moving first, so the wise general waits.
In narrow passes, occupy the pass first and fill it with a strong force. If the enemy is already there in strength, do not follow him in, but if his force is weak, you may attack.
On steep heights, take the sunny side first and wait for the enemy there. If the enemy is far away and equal in strength, it is hard to start a battle, so do not try.
Sun Tzu says that the shape of the land is a soldier's best ally. The test of a great general, however, is to judge his enemy and to calculate dangers and distances wisely.
Sun Tzu names six kinds of disaster that may happen to an army. They are flight, insubordination, collapse, ruin, disorganisation and rout, and the fault is the general's, not nature's.

If a small force attacks one ten times larger, the result is flight. If the soldiers are strong but the officers are weak, the result is insubordination, and if the reverse is true, the army collapses.
Ruin happens when angry officers fight on their own without orders. Disorganisation comes from a weak general with unclear orders, and rout comes from sending a weak force against a strong one.
A general who advances without seeking fame and retreats without fear of shame is a jewel for his kingdom. He thinks only of protecting his country, and of serving his ruler well.

Sun Tzu says that a commander who treats his soldiers like his own children will be followed into the deepest valleys. But kindness alone is not enough, because soldiers who are never corrected become like spoiled children.
In the chapter on the nine situations, Sun Tzu names nine kinds of ground. The first is dispersive ground, which is fought in your own land, where the soldiers think of home and may run away.

Facile ground is when you have gone only a little way into enemy country, and here you should not stop. Contentious ground is a place that both sides want, and it should not be attacked if the enemy has already taken it.
On open ground, where both sides can move freely, do not try to block the enemy. On ground where many roads meet, join hands with your allies.

On serious ground, you have gone deep into the enemy's land, leaving many walled towns behind you, and you should gather food there. On difficult ground, such as mountains, forests and marshes, you should keep moving.
On hemmed-in ground, which has a narrow way in and a winding way out, use stratagem. On desperate ground, where you can survive only by fighting at once, you must fight.
Sun Tzu says that clever leaders of long ago made the enemy's front and rear lose touch with each other. They also stopped his large and small groups from helping one another.
Sun Tzu is asked what to do about a large, well-ordered army that is about to attack. He answers that you should begin by seizing something the enemy holds dear.
Sun Tzu says that rapidity is the essence of war. We should take advantage of the enemy's lack of readiness and travel by roads he does not expect.
The farther an army goes into enemy country, the more united it becomes, and the defenders cannot beat it. It should make use of fertile land to feed itself, and look after its men carefully.
Sun Tzu says that a general should keep his army constantly on the move. He should make plans that nobody can see through, so the enemy cannot guess the next step.
Sun Tzu says that if soldiers are put where there is no escape, they will prefer death to running away. If they are ready to face death, there is nothing they cannot do.
Soldiers in desperate danger lose all sense of fear. If there is no place to run, they stand firm, and if there is no help for it, they fight hard.
Without waiting to be told, soldiers in this position will be watchful and loyal. Sun Tzu says to forbid omens and superstitious doubts, and then no disaster need be feared.
Soldiers are not against wealth or long life, Sun Tzu says. On the day they are ordered to fight, some may weep, but cornered, they show the courage of heroes.
Sun Tzu compares a skilful army to a snake on a famous mountain. Strike its head and the tail attacks you, and strike its tail and the head attacks you.
The men of Wu and Yue were bitter enemies. Yet in one boat in a storm, they helped each other like a left hand and a right hand.
It is not enough to tie up the horses and bury the wheels of the wagons. The best way to manage an army is to set one level of courage that everyone must reach.
A skilful general leads his army as if he were leading one man by the hand. He must be calm to keep secrets and fair to keep order.
At the right moment, a leader is like a man who climbs a height and then kicks away the ladder. He burns his boats and breaks his cooking pots, so his men can go only forward.
Sun Tzu says to begin by being as shy as a young woman, until the enemy gives you an opening. Then be as quick as a running hare, and the enemy will have no time to answer.
In the chapter on the attack by fire, Sun Tzu names five targets for fire. They are the soldiers' camp, the food stores, the baggage wagons, the weapon stores and the enemy's army itself.
To carry out an attack by fire, we need the means to do it. The materials for starting a fire must always be kept ready.
There is a right time of year for fire, when the weather is very dry. The special days are when the moon is in four star groups, which are signs of rising wind.
Sun Tzu says to be ready for five developments after a fire. When a fire breaks out inside the enemy camp, you should attack from outside at once.
When the fire is at its height, follow with an attack if you can. If you cannot, stay where you are, and when you start a fire, be on the side the wind comes from.
A wind that rises in the daytime lasts for a long time, but a breeze at night soon falls. Every army must know the five developments and watch the stars for the right days.
Sun Tzu says that those who use fire to help their attack show intelligence, and those who use water gain strength. Water can cut off an enemy, but it cannot take everything from him.
Sun Tzu says that winning battles without a clear aim leads to a waste of time. A wise ruler makes his plans well in advance, and a good general builds up his resources.
Sun Tzu says to move only when you see an advantage. Use your troops only when there is something to gain, and fight only when the position is really critical.
No ruler should start a war just because he is angry, and no general should fight just out of spite. Anger can turn to gladness, but a destroyed kingdom can never come back.
In the chapter on the use of spies, Sun Tzu says that a big army on a long march is a huge cost. It costs a thousand pieces of silver a day, and it stops many families from working.
Armies may face each other for years, waiting for a victory that is decided in a single day. To stay in ignorance of the enemy just to save a little silver, Sun Tzu says, is very unkind.
A ruler who will not pay for information is no real leader, Sun Tzu says. What lets a wise ruler and a good general win is knowing things before they happen.
Sun Tzu says that knowledge of the enemy cannot come from spirits or from old experience. It can only come from other people who really know the situation.
Sun Tzu names five kinds of spies: local, inside, double, doomed and living. When all five are at work, he says, no one can find out how the system works.
Local spies are the people who live in the enemy's district, and we use their knowledge. Inside spies are the enemy's own officials, who tell us what they know.
Double spies are enemy spies whom we win over. Doomed spies are given false news to pass to the enemy, and living spies bring us back the news from the enemy's camp.
No one in the army is closer to the general than the spies. None should be rewarded more generously, and no work is more secret.
Be subtle, Sun Tzu says, and use spies in every kind of business. If a secret is told before the right time, the harm is great, so secrets must be kept with great care.
Sun Tzu says that the double spy is the most important of the five. Through him we learn about the enemy's country and can find local and inside spies.
The thirteen chapters of the book are now finished, and its shape is clear. The book began with a warning that war is serious, and it ends with the lesson that good knowledge is the best weapon.
For many centuries, people copied the book by hand. About 1,800 years ago, a famous warlord named Cao Cao wrote notes on it, and many scholars followed him.
In 1972, bamboo strips with the text of The Art of War were found in a tomb at Yinqueshan. The tomb is about two thousand years old, and this showed that the book is very old.
The book travelled to Japan, where soldiers and leaders studied it. A sixteenth-century warlord named Takeda Shingen put its saying about wind, forest, fire and mountain on his banners.
In 1772, a missionary named Amiot published the first translation of the book into a European language, French. Many other translations followed in the centuries after that, in many languages.
Today, soldiers are not the only people who read the book. Business people, coaches, lawyers and students use its ideas to plan their work and to compete wisely.
Many famous lines that are said to be by Sun Tzu cannot be found in the book. A careful reader should check a quotation before believing it.
The book comes from a world of chariots and city walls, so a modern reader should use judgement. It is also humane, since it praises restraint and kindness to prisoners.
In everyday life, too, the best result is often the one that needs no fight. A quiet plan, a patient word and careful preparation can solve many problems before they begin.

The Art of War is still read today by soldiers, teachers, athletes and business people. Its main lesson is that careful thinking and preparation matter more than force, and that the best victory is the one that avoids a battle.
C1C2: The Art of War is a short Chinese book on strategy, and it has been read for roughly two and a half thousand years by generals, rulers and, more recently, business leaders and athletes.
