Tradition credits it to Sun Tzu, a military thinker of the ancient Chinese states, although scholars still argue about who he was and exactly when the text took its present form. Whatever its origins, it endures because its subject is not really fighting at all, but the clearer thinking that lets a person avoid a fight, or win it cheaply.

The world that produced this book was a patchwork of rival Chinese states, each ruled by a king or a duke who watched his neighbours with suspicion. Wars were frequent, armies were growing larger, and a single defeat could wipe a whole state from the map. In such an age, a book that taught rulers how to win without ruin was bound to find readers.

Nearly everything told about the life of Sun Tzu comes from Sima Qian, a Chinese historian who wrote about two thousand years ago, long after the man himself would have died. According to him, Sun Tzu, came from the state of Qi and was known for his skill in the art of war. Some modern scholars doubt parts of the story, so it is best read as a tradition and not as settled history.

According to the old story, Sun Tzu left his home and travelled to Wu, a state in the south, where King Helü was looking for men of talent. He brought with him thirteen short chapters on the art of war, which he offered to the king as proof of what he could do. The king read them with interest, but a book, he suspected, is one thing and an army is quite another.

King Helü told Sun Tzu that he had read the chapters with pleasure, but he wanted to see their lessons put to the test. To make the test as hard as possible, and perhaps a little amusing, he proposed that Sun Tzu should drill the women of his palace as though they were an army. Sun Tzu accepted without hesitation, which suggests that he was quite sure of his method.

Sun Tzu gathered the women, who numbered about one hundred and eighty in the story, and divided them into two companies. He named the king's two favourite ladies as their captains, and gave each woman a spear so that the drill would look like the real thing. Choosing the favourites was a bold step, since it showed that nobody would be allowed to stand above the rules.

Before anything began, Sun Tzu made sure that every woman understood what the words right, left, front and back would mean, and he repeated the instructions several times. Only when he was satisfied that nobody could be confused did he give the signal on the drum for the women to turn to the right. The women, who thought the whole business was only a game, burst into helpless laughter.

Sun Tzu reasoned that if the orders had not been clear, the fault was the general's, and so he explained everything once more and beat the drum again. When the women laughed a second time, he decided that the orders were clear and that the fault must lie with the officers, and the two captains were condemned. The king watched in horror and sent a message begging for mercy, but Sun Tzu replied that a general in the field does not have to obey every command from his ruler.

With two new captains in place, the drill began for the third time, and the effect was astonishing. The women turned and marched, knelt and stood, with the exactness of seasoned soldiers, and not one of them dared to utter a sound or look to the side. Sun Tzu then sent word to the king that his troops were ready, and that they would go through fire and water at the king's command.

The king, still grieving for his favourites, told Sun Tzu to rest in his quarters, and he declined to come and see the troops. In time, however, he understood that Sun Tzu was a man who really knew how to command, and he appointed him as a general. The tradition adds that Wu then defeated the powerful state of Chu, though historians admit that they cannot be certain how much of the story is true.

Sun Tzu opens his book with a warning: war is the greatest affair of a state, the ground on which lives are saved or lost and a nation either survives or vanishes. For that reason, he insists, it can never be left to impulse, pride or anger, but must be examined from every side. A ruler who goes to war without first studying it deeply is gambling with the lives of everyone he governs.

Sun Tzu says that every war rests on five factors, which he calls the way, heaven, earth, the commander and method. A ruler who understands all five has already done half the work of winning, and one who ignores even a single factor is moving blindly. Each of them, as the next pages show, is a question that must be answered honestly before a single soldier marches.

By the way, Sun Tzu means the bond of shared purpose between a ruler and his people. When the ruler is just and the people believe in him, they will follow him into danger as though they had no fear of death. An army that fights for something it believes in has an advantage that no amount of cleverness elsewhere can replace.

Heaven, in Sun Tzu's language, covers all that belongs to time and the sky: night and day, cold and heat, and the slow turning of the seasons. An army that marches in the wrong season may be beaten by the weather before it ever meets an enemy. A wise commander therefore reads the calendar as carefully as he reads a map.

Earth is the third factor, and it takes in distance, height, breadth and every kind of ground, from open plains to narrow passes where a few men can stop a crowd. A commander who has studied the land knows where to stand, where to hide and where a march will cost more than it can gain. The leader who is a stranger to the country he fights in has given his enemy a gift.

The fourth factor is the commander himself, who must combine wisdom, trustworthiness, kindness, courage and strictness. These qualities pull against each other, so the real skill lies in balance: too much kindness makes an army soft, and too much strictness makes it afraid. A plan is only as good as the person who has to carry it out.

The last factor, method, is the practical machinery of an army: its ranks and divisions, its rules, the roads it uses and the supplies that feed it. Courage and cunning count for little when soldiers are hungry, orders are confused or nobody knows who is in charge. Good organisation is dull to look at, but it is the quiet foundation of every victory.

Every general, Sun Tzu remarks, has heard of these five factors, and almost any of them could repeat the list from memory. Knowing the words is not the same as understanding the thing, however, and it is the commander who studies each factor honestly who wins, while the one who merely recites them is defeated. The lesson is an old one: a famous idea is useless until somebody puts it to work.

In those days a ruler would go to the temple of his ancestors, in the quiet of a solemn place, to make his calculations before a campaign. Sun Tzu observes that the general who wins a battle has usually made many such calculations before it began, while the general who loses has made few. The real contest, in other words, is often decided in a quiet room, long before the first arrow flies.

Sun Tzu closes this part of the chapter with a note of quiet confidence, telling his ruler that a general who listens to his advice and acts upon it will conquer, and should therefore be kept in command. The general who ignores the counsel, by the same reasoning, will suffer defeat and should be dismissed. It is a bold claim for a book to make about itself, though the careful reader may judge whether the rest of its pages earn it.

Next, Sun Tzu proposes seven questions that can be asked about any two armies before they meet, and he says the answers will reveal where victory is likely to lie. The questions are practical ones, as simple as the questions a doctor asks before he examines a patient. They turn a vague feeling about the future into a careful comparison, which is the habit he wants every commander to learn.

The first question concerns the rulers: which of them rules in harmony with his people, so that they trust him and will follow him into hardship? The second concerns the generals, and asks which of them has the greater ability, since a gifted general may achieve more with an ordinary army than a poor one can with a splendid force. Both of these questions look first at people, and this is where Sun Tzu always begins his thinking.

The third question asks which side has the advantage of heaven and earth, meaning the better season, the better weather and the stronger ground. The fourth asks on which side the rules of the army are enforced most strictly, since a force that obeys its orders in small matters will usually obey them in large ones. Discipline, in Sun Tzu's eyes, is not a punishment but a source of strength that the enemy can see.

The fifth question is a simple matter of strength: which army has the greater force, in men, weapons and equipment, when everything is counted honestly? The sixth asks on which side the officers and men have been better trained, for training turns a crowd of strong people into an army that can carry out an order. Numbers alone, Sun Tzu implies, are a poor guide unless they are put together with skill.

The final question is about fairness: on which side are rewards and punishments given most consistently, so that every soldier knows what to expect for good and bad conduct? A reward that arrives only when it is convenient, or a punishment that falls only on the weak, quickly teaches an army to stop trying. Fairness, being a form of trust, is part of what holds men together under pressure.

From these questions, Sun Tzu claims, he can foresee who will win and who will lose, because careful calculation favours victory and carelessness favours defeat. He then asks, in a sentence that is almost a joke, what chance there can be for the commander who makes no calculation whatever. His point is that a war entered without counting the cost is not a plan at all, but only a hope.

All warfare, Sun Tzu declares, is based on deception, and a skilled commander hides the truth about his own side from the enemy. The enemy who believes the false picture will make his plans on a mistake, which is the greatest gift a commander can receive. It is worth remembering that Sun Tzu is writing about armies and rivals in a hard world, and not about how a person should treat friends.

When he is strong, the skilled commander appears weak, and when he is ready he appears careless, and when he intends to move he seems to be standing still. In the same way, when he is close to the enemy he gives the impression of being far away, and when he is far he seems to be near. The enemy, deceived about all these things, cannot judge what is really happening in front of him.

Sun Tzu advises that a little bait may draw the enemy forward, and that where his ranks are in confusion, a commander may take the chance to strike. If the enemy is strong in every way, one should be fully ready for him, and if he is simply too strong, one should keep out of his way. These are the habits of a person who plays for the long term and who does not mind losing a small thing to win a great one.

If the enemy is quick to anger, Sun Tzu says, one may stir him up until he forgets to think, and if he is proud, one may flatter him with a show of weakness. If he is resting one must give him no peace, and if his men are united one must find a way to divide them, always striking where he is unprepared. The secrets of victory, he adds, cannot be told in advance, for they must be found in the moment itself.

The second chapter begins by painting a picture of an army in the field, and the picture is a very large one: a thousand fast chariots, a thousand heavy ones and a hundred thousand soldiers in armour. Such a force must be fed and equipped for a march of hundreds of miles, and none of this comes free. Before a single fight has begun, the ruler has already taken on a mountain of expense.

Sun Tzu reckons that keeping such an army in the field costs a thousand pieces of silver every day, a sum that is spent both at home and at the front. The list of expenses seems endless, running from the food for the men and the visits of foreign guests to humble things like glue, paint and the materials for repairing chariots and armour. Only when all this money has been found, he says, can the army set out at all.

Sun Tzu observes that when victory is slow in coming, the weapons grow blunt and the spirits of the soldiers grow damp. If the army is then ordered to besiege a walled city, it will use up the last of its strength against stone walls, and the whole state will feel the strain. A campaign that drags on is therefore rather like a fire that burns up its own fuel.

When an army is worn out and the treasury is empty, Sun Tzu warns, the neighbouring rulers will see their chance and move in against the weakened state. At that point no adviser, however wise, can avert the consequences, because the damage was done long before and cannot be undone by cleverness. He knows of no case, he says, in which a country gained from a war that went on for a long time.

For Sun Tzu, speed is worth more than polish: a plain victory won quickly is better than an elegant one that takes years to complete. Every extra month spent in the field costs lives and money and gives the enemy time to recover, so the wise commander aims to finish the matter swiftly. This does not mean rushing without thought, but acting once the plan is ready and the moment has come.

Only the man who understands the dangers of war, Sun Tzu argues, can fully understand how to make it pay, since knowing the harm is the first step toward avoiding it. The skilful commander does not raise a second army or load his supply wagons a third time, for each extra effort multiplies the cost without improving the result. He carries what he needs from home at the start, and he takes the rest from the enemy.

A clever commander, Sun Tzu advises, makes the enemy's country feed his army, because hauling supplies over long roads is ruinously expensive and slow. He says that a single cartload taken from the enemy is worth about twenty carried from home, since the carrying itself eats up so much of the load. In this way an army lowers its own costs while it lowers the enemy's strength as well.

When an army must be supplied from a distance, Sun Tzu points out, the people are made poor by the burden of carrying the goods. Prices also rise wherever an army is camped, so that families near the soldiers find their savings drained away, and the tax collector then takes from those who have little left. A war that is won in the field may thus be lost quietly in the villages.

To keep the soldiers eager, Sun Tzu recommends giving a reward to the man who first seizes ten or more chariots from the enemy. The captured vehicles should then be marked with the army's own flags, mixed in with its own chariots and put to work at once. In this way the enemy's strength becomes the victor's strength, and the whole business pays for itself.

Soldiers captured from the enemy, Sun Tzu says, should be treated kindly and kept, so that they may in time serve under the victor's own flags. He calls this winning a battle and growing stronger at the same time, because the conquest adds to the army instead of only subtracting from the enemy. The chapter ends with a reminder that the true aim of war is victory and not endless fighting, and that a good general holds the fate of the people in his hands.

The third chapter contains Sun Tzu's most famous idea, which is that the best victory is to take an enemy's country whole and undamaged rather than to smash it. Winning a hundred battles is not the highest skill, he says, for the highest skill is to break the enemy's will to resist without fighting at all. Destruction is expensive and leaves a mess that the winner must clean up, while a bloodless victory leaves the prize intact.

The principle holds at every scale, Sun Tzu says, from a whole army down to a regiment, a company or a squad of five. It is always better to capture such a body in good order than to destroy it, since an intact prize may be put to use and a destroyed one only leaves bitterness. The best fighters are therefore those who win by persuading and surrounding, and not by smashing.

Sun Tzu sets out the ways of fighting in a ladder, with the best at the top and the worst at the bottom. Highest of all is to attack the enemy's plans while they are still plans, so that no army ever has to march and no fight ever has to begin. A mind that anticipates trouble can often stop it for the price of a few quiet words.

The second-best method, Sun Tzu says, is to break up the enemy's alliances, so that he can no longer rely on friends for supplies, soldiers or advice. A ruler who has been left alone must defend every border himself and cannot call anyone to his aid. Diplomacy of this kind is cheaper than an army, and its results can be just as complete.

Third in the ranking comes the pitched battle, in which two armies meet in the open and one of them breaks, and it is already expensive in lives and in money. Lowest of all is the assault on a walled city, which Sun Tzu advises only when there is no alternative at all. The lower the rung of the ladder, the heavier the cost, which is why a thoughtful commander tries to win on the upper steps.

Sun Tzu points out that a siege cannot be begun in a hurry, since the shields, covered shelters and other machines of war take about three months to prepare. A further three months may be needed to pile up earth against the walls so that the attackers can climb them. During those six months the enemy is not idle, and neither is the clock that is counting the army's expenses.

The general who cannot master his own impatience, Sun Tzu says, sends his soldiers swarming up the walls like a column of ants. The result is that perhaps a third of the army is lost, and the city still has not fallen. This is what comes of attacking a wall because a plan has failed, and the lesson is that anger is a very expensive adviser.

The skilled commander, in Sun Tzu's picture, subdues the enemy's army without a battle, captures his cities without a siege and ends the war without a long campaign. He takes everything under heaven whole and undamaged, so that his army is not worn down and his gain is complete. A victory of this kind makes little noise, and so it rarely makes a hero of the person who wins it.

Since the clever commander has used neither his army nor his treasury, he can turn at once to the larger prize and compete for leadership of all the land. His soldiers are fresh, his stores are full and his reputation is untouched, so his triumph is complete and no part of it has been spent. This, Sun Tzu says, is the method of attacking by stratagem, and it is a method that few leaders have ever mastered.

Sun Tzu then turns to numbers and gives a few clear rules: with ten times the enemy's strength, surround him, and with five times, attack him. With twice as many men one should divide his army and strike at its parts, and if the two sides are equal, one may fight if one is able. A slightly weaker force should avoid battle, and a very weak one should simply slip away, because a small army that fights stubbornly will only be captured by a larger one.

The commander, Sun Tzu says, is the support of the state, like the frame of a cart that holds the wheels in place. When his abilities are complete, the state will be strong, and when they have gaps, the state will be weak. A ruler should therefore choose his general with the same care that he gives to choosing his own heir.

A ruler, Sun Tzu warns, can bring misfortune on his own army in three ways, the first of which is to command it to advance or to retreat without knowing what is happening on the ground. The second is to govern it as though it were a court, forgetting that its rules and its needs are quite different, and the third is to give posts to officers without judging whether they are fit for them. In each case the ruler has taken a habit that works in the palace and wrongly applied it to the field.

When an army is made restless and doubtful by such mistakes, Sun Tzu says, the neighbouring rulers will bring trouble, and the army will be beaten before the enemy has even arrived. He calls this bringing disorder into the army and throwing victory away, and it is the worst kind of defeat. A force that has been confused by its own side is already half beaten, and the enemy has only to finish the work.

Sun Tzu lists five signs by which a victor may be known: he knows when to fight and when to hold back, and he understands how to use both large forces and small. His ranks share a single spirit, he is prepared while his enemy is not, and he has a capable general whom the ruler does not interfere with. Where all five of these signs are present, he says, victory may be confidently expected.

Here is the line that has made the book famous: if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, you will win some and lose some, and if you know neither, every battle will be a danger to you. The advice sounds simple, but the second half, knowing oneself honestly, is the harder task.

In the fourth chapter, on the placing of an army, Sun Tzu teaches that the skilled leader first puts himself beyond the possibility of defeat and then waits for the enemy to make himself beatable. Whether one can avoid defeat depends on one's own preparation, but whether one can win depends on the enemy's mistakes. Patience is therefore a form of strength, since no one can force a victory that the other side has not yet allowed.

Defence, Sun Tzu explains, is the right course when strength is lacking, and attack is the right course when strength is plentiful. The master of defence hides himself as if he were buried in the deepest part of the earth, while the master of attack strikes as if from the highest part of the sky. Between these two styles there is no cowardice and no boldness, only the sensible use of what one actually has.

To foresee a victory that any common person can foresee, says Sun Tzu, is not the height of skill, and to win a famous battle that the whole world applauds is not either. Lifting a feather is no proof of strength, he points out, and noticing the sun and moon is no proof of sharp sight, nor is hearing thunder a sign of a quick ear. The truly skilled fighter wins where winning is easy, because he has already removed every difficulty, and so his victories bring neither fame nor praise.

A victorious army, according to Sun Tzu, secures its victory first and only afterwards goes to battle, while a defeated army fights first and then looks for a way to win. The difference lies in the preparation, which is done quietly and well before a single weapon is raised. Where the preparation is thorough, the fighting is mostly a formality, and where it is missing, no amount of courage will make up for it.

A winning army set against a losing one, Sun Tzu says, is like a heavy weight placed in the scale against a single grain, and the outcome is never in doubt. Such an army moves like water that has been held back behind a dam and then released into a deep gorge, and nothing in its path can stand against it. The picture is a fitting end to the chapter, for it shows that victory comes from the work done before the gate is opened.

The fifth chapter, on energy, begins with the observation that controlling many men is the same in principle as controlling a few, so long as they are divided into units of the right size. Each unit has its own leader, and each leader answers to the one above him, so that an order passes down the chain like water along a channel. A crowd becomes an army only when it is organised, and no amount of courage can replace that organisation.

A large army can be fought as though it were a single man, Sun Tzu says, so long as clear signals tell everyone what to do and when to do it. Drums and gongs serve in the noise of battle, where soldiers cannot see their leaders, and banners and flags serve where the noise is too great for the voice to carry. The signal is the thread that ties thousands of separate wills into one purpose.

To make an army able to face the enemy's attack and remain unshaken, Sun Tzu says, a commander needs two kinds of action, the direct and the indirect. The direct force holds the enemy's attention at the front, and the indirect force comes from an unexpected direction at the moment when he has committed himself. A battle is joined by the first, he says, and won by the second.

The possibilities of the indirect method, Sun Tzu says, are as endless as heaven and earth and as inexhaustible as the flow of rivers. Like the sun and moon, they set only to rise again, and like the four seasons, they pass away only to return. A commander who understands this need never fear that he will run out of ideas.

Sun Tzu points out that the musical scale of his day had only five notes, and yet their combinations produce more melodies than anyone could ever listen to. He uses this plain fact to show how a small number of simple elements can create an endless variety of results. In war, as in music, the artist is the one who knows how to combine the notes.

He adds that there are no more than five primary colours and five basic tastes, yet these few things give rise to more shades than the eye can count and more flavours than the tongue can learn. The reasoning is the same as before: from a short list of simple elements, skilful mixing brings an endless supply of new things. Surprise, he implies, is a matter of using the same tools in a new order.

In battle there are only the direct and the indirect, Sun Tzu says, yet the two give rise to each other in an unending cycle, like a ring that has neither beginning nor end. What was a direct attack a moment ago becomes the cover for an indirect one, and the surprise of one hour is the expected move of the next. No one, he asks, can ever exhaust the combinations of such a simple and powerful thing.

The quality of decision, Sun Tzu says, is like the swoop of a falcon that strikes and kills its prey at exactly the right instant. The energy of a good attack is like the slow drawing of a crossbow, and the decision itself is like the sudden release of the trigger. Everything depends on the patience that gathers the force and the judgement that chooses the moment to let it go.

Sun Tzu says that amid the confusion of battle there must be no true disorder, for an army that is truly confused is already lost. To act out disorder, in order to fool the enemy, requires perfect discipline, just as pretending to be afraid requires courage and pretending to be weak requires strength. A good actor in war must therefore first be a very good and very disciplined soldier.

The skilful commander, Sun Tzu says, looks for victory from the combined energy of his army and not from the efforts of single men. He uses his troops as one might roll round stones down a steep mountain, where a square stone would remain still and a round one would gather speed. The art lies in giving the army the right shape and putting it in the right place, and then letting the slope do the work.

In the sixth chapter, Sun Tzu points out that whoever occupies the field first and awaits the enemy there will be fresh, while whoever arrives second and rushes into battle will be exhausted. The skilled commander therefore draws the enemy to him and is never drawn to the enemy, so that the tired side always belongs to the other camp. In this way he controls the pace of the fight without raising his voice.

The skilful fighter, in Sun Tzu's words, imposes his will upon the enemy and does not allow the enemy's will to be imposed upon himself. He chooses the place, the hour and the shape of the contest, so that the enemy is always responding and never leading. It is the difference between a player who makes the moves and a player who is merely moved.

By holding out a prospect of gain, Sun Tzu says, a commander can draw the enemy toward him, and by threatening some damage he can make it impossible for him to come near. In both cases the commander is using the enemy's own wishes and fears to move him, as a herdsman moves a cow with grass or a stick. The enemy's mind, and not merely his body, is the real battlefield of any war.

If the enemy is at his ease, Sun Tzu advises, he can be worn down by constant harassment, and if he is well fed, he can be starved by cutting his supplies. If he is encamped quietly in a place he likes, he should be forced to move, since comfort is a kind of strength that can be taken away. In every case the aim is to turn the enemy's advantage into a burden.

Appear at those points, Sun Tzu advises, which the enemy must hasten to defend, and march swiftly to places where he does not expect you. A threat that calls the enemy to one side leaves another side open, and it costs the attacker little to make the threat. The result is an enemy who spends the whole campaign running to the wrong place.

An army may march for a great distance without distress, says Sun Tzu, so long as it travels through country where the enemy is not. This is a plain truth, but it contains a deeper idea: a skilful commander does not push through opposition but chooses a road on which opposition does not exist. To be strong is good, but to arrive without having to be strong is better.

An army, Sun Tzu says, will take whatever it attacks if it attacks what is not defended, and it will hold whatever it defends if it defends what cannot be attacked. The master of attack leaves his rival not knowing where to defend, and the master of defence leaves him not knowing where to attack. Between them, these two skills make a commander who is never surprised and always the one to surprise.

How divine is the art of subtlety and secrecy, Sun Tzu exclaims, for it allows a general to become invisible and inaudible and thus hold the fate of the enemy in his hands. An enemy who cannot see his opponent cannot guess his plan, and one who cannot hear him cannot prepare for his arrival. The greatest commanders, then, are the ones whom the enemy never quite manages to find.

You may advance and be absolutely irresistible, Sun Tzu says, if you make for the weak points of the enemy, and you may retreat in safety if your movements are quicker than his. Speed and attention to weakness are the two sides of the same skill, one used in attack and the other in withdrawal. Neither requires a larger army, only a better understanding of where the enemy is soft and when he will move.

If we wish to fight, Sun Tzu says, the enemy can be forced to battle even behind a high wall and a deep ditch, simply by attacking a place that he cannot afford to lose. If we do not wish to fight, we can prevent the battle even though our camp is only a line drawn on the ground, by putting something strange and unexplained in his way. The commander who controls whether and when the fight happens has already won the first round.

By discovering the enemy's dispositions while remaining invisible ourselves, Sun Tzu says, we can keep our forces concentrated while his must be divided. The enemy who does not know where we shall strike has no choice but to guard everywhere, and a force that guards everywhere is weak everywhere. Secrecy thus buys us the thing that every commander wants most, which is the power to choose where to fight.

If we are united and the enemy is split into fractions, Sun Tzu says, we can bring our whole strength against a single part of his army, and so we are many against few. Even if our army is the smaller one in total, it will be the larger one at the place where the fight actually happens. This is the arithmetic of concentration, and it is more important than the arithmetic of numbers.

The spot where we intend to fight must not be made known, Sun Tzu says, for then the enemy has to prepare against several possible attacks, and his forces are thinly spread. The more points he must defend, the fewer men he will have at any one of them, and the easier it will be for us to break through. A secret kept well is therefore worth more than a whole regiment of soldiers.

If the enemy strengthens his front, Sun Tzu says, he will weaken his rear, and if he strengthens his left, he will weaken his right, since no commander can be strong everywhere. Weakness in numbers comes from having to guard against possible attacks, while strength in numbers comes from making the enemy guard against us. The more places a ruler has to protect, the more of his army is wasted on waiting.

If we know where and when a battle will be fought, Sun Tzu says, our forces may gather from afar and arrive together, but if we do not know, the left wing cannot help the right. He then turns to the rival states of Wu and Yue and remarks that though Yue may have more soldiers, this will not bring it victory. Numbers are worth nothing unless they can be put in the right place at the right time.

Rouse the enemy, Sun Tzu advises, and learn the principle of his activity or inactivity, and force him to reveal himself so that his weak places can be seen. Then compare his army carefully with your own, so that you know where your strength is more than enough and where it falls short. A commander who tests before he commits acts like a doctor who feels the pulse before he gives any medicine.

In arranging an army, Sun Tzu says, the highest skill is to be formless, so that the subtlest spy cannot learn anything and the wisest adviser cannot make a plan against you. All men can see the tactics by which a commander wins, he adds, but nobody can see the strategy out of which the victory was made. What is visible is only the surface of the sea, and the real work is done in the depths.

A tactic that has won one battle, Sun Tzu cautions, should not simply be repeated in the next, for the circumstances of war are endlessly various. The commander who learns only one lesson from his success is a poor student, because the enemy has probably learned something too. Methods must therefore be regulated by the situation, and never by habit or pride.

Military tactics, Sun Tzu says, are like water, which runs away from high places and hurries to the low ground. An army likewise avoids the strong and strikes at the weak, going around obstacles instead of battering them and filling every gap that is left open. The power of water is not its hardness but its refusal to meet a wall with another wall.

As water shapes its course according to the ground over which it flows, so a soldier works out his victory in relation to the foe he faces, and there are no constant conditions in war. The commander who can modify his tactics to suit his opponent and so win may be called a heaven-born captain, for he has learned the lesson that the seasons and the moon teach us all. Day follows night, and the moon grows full and then thin again, and nothing in war stays in one shape for long.

The seventh chapter, on manoeuvring, begins with the general's duties after he receives his commands from the ruler. He must gather his army, make its parts work together in harmony, and then camp it in a good place before any fighting can begin. Only then, Sun Tzu says, comes the most difficult part of the whole business, which is moving the army about in the face of the enemy.

The difficulty of tactical manoeuvring, Sun Tzu says, is to turn a long and roundabout road into a short one, and to turn bad luck into good. A clever commander sets out after his enemy and arrives before him, by making the enemy believe that the road is longer than it is, or by offering him something that leads him astray. In the end, skill with distance turns out to be skill with the mind of the other side.

Manoeuvring with a disciplined army, Sun Tzu says, is a great advantage, but manoeuvring with an undisciplined crowd is among the most dangerous things that a commander can try. A force without order will lose its way, lose its temper and lose its nerve at exactly the moment when it needs all three. The same bold plan may bring glory to one general and disaster to another, depending only on the quality of the men who carry it out.

If an army is set in motion with all its equipment in order to snatch an advantage, Sun Tzu warns, the chances are that it will arrive too late. If, on the other hand, a fast column is sent ahead for the purpose, it must sacrifice its baggage and its stores, and a force that has left its food behind is in trouble from the start. Every choice in war has a price, and the art is to know which price is worth paying.

Speed has a price, warns Sun Tzu, and an army driven on a forced march without rest, day and night, arrives scattered and spent, with the strong in front and the tired far behind. After a very long march of this kind, he says, perhaps only one man in ten will reach the goal in a fit state, and the generals themselves may be captured. The art lies in moving swiftly without breaking the very thing that is doing the moving.

An army that has no baggage train is lost, says Sun Tzu, and so is an army that has no food, and so is an army that has no stores or safe bases from which to draw supplies. The point is a plain one but easily forgotten in the excitement of a campaign, when everyone wants to talk about victory and nobody wants to talk about bread. A commander who studies the supply line as carefully as the battle line has understood the first rule of war.

We cannot lead an army on the march, Sun Tzu says, unless we are familiar with the face of the country, with its mountains and forests, its cliffs and precipices, its marshes and swamps. Where we lack that knowledge, we must use local guides, for a man who has lived all his life in a district knows things that no map can tell. To march blind into the enemy's country is a way of volunteering to be surprised.

Move only if there is an advantage to be gained, Sun Tzu advises, and decide by circumstances whether to gather the troops or divide them. When a country is plundered, the spoil should be shared among the men, and when new land is taken it should be divided among them for their benefit, since a reward that is promised and kept makes an army loyal. The commander is wise to weigh each move before he makes it, and not afterwards.

He will conquer, Sun Tzu says, who has learned the art of making the roundabout way a direct one, and this is the true art of manoeuvring. It is a skill that combines imagination with timing, since it needs both the cunning to choose the odd road and the discipline to follow it to the end. The prize goes not to the strongest army but to the one that understands distance.

Sun Tzu quotes an old book on the management of armies, which says that on the field of battle the spoken word does not carry far enough, and so gongs and drums were invented. In the same way, ordinary objects are hard to see in the confusion, and so banners and flags were introduced. These things are the ears and eyes of the army, and they allow one mind to direct thousands of bodies.

Sun Tzu describes the ideal army by a series of images, of which the first is the rapidity of the wind. The second is the compactness of a forest, in which the trees stand close together and make no sound. An army that can be fast when speed is needed and still when stillness is needed has already learned half its trade.

In raiding and taking spoil, Sun Tzu continues, an army should be like fire, which spreads quickly and leaves nothing behind it. In holding its ground, it should be like a mountain, which does not move however hard the wind blows. These are opposite qualities, and the point of the image is that a good commander has both and knows which of them to use.

Let your plans be dark and impenetrable as night, says Sun Tzu, and when you move, fall like a thunderbolt. The point of the image is the contrast between a long silence and a sudden crash, since the enemy hears nothing until the moment when he can do nothing. Together with the other images, this makes the picture of an army that knows when to hide and when to be seen.

Gongs and drums, banners and flags, are the means by which the eyes and ears of the whole army are fixed on one point. When the army moves as a single united body, Sun Tzu says, the brave man cannot advance alone and the coward cannot retreat alone, since everyone is carried along by the others. This is the way to manage large numbers of men, and it is much more reliable than hoping that each man will do his duty.

In night fighting, Sun Tzu says, an army should make great use of signal fires and drums, and in fighting by day it should use flags and banners in large numbers. In each case the means are chosen to suit the senses, so as to direct the ears and eyes of the army in the way that conditions permit. The aim is always the same, which is to make sure that thousands of men understand the same message at the same moment.

A whole army, Sun Tzu observes, may be robbed of its spirit, and the commander in chief may be robbed of his presence of mind. An army that is afraid fights badly, and a general who is shaken makes poor decisions, so the two weaknesses feed each other. The clever attacker therefore aims at the courage of the enemy as much as at his walls and his weapons.

A soldier's spirit, Sun Tzu observes, is keenest in the morning, begins to flag by noonday and by the evening is bent only on returning to camp. A clever general therefore avoids an army when its spirit is keen and attacks it when it is sluggish and ready to go home. The skill is to read the rhythm of the day as a musician reads the beat.

Sun Tzu advises meeting disorder with discipline and clamour with calm, and this he calls the art of mastering self-control. To be near the goal while the enemy is still far from it, to be rested while he is worn out and to be well fed while he is hungry is the art of husbanding strength. The calm side wins because the other side has already spent its strength on noise.

Sun Tzu gives a list of things not to do: do not intercept an enemy whose banners are in perfect order, and do not attack troops who are drawn up in calm and confident array. Do not march uphill against the enemy or oppose him when he comes downhill, do not pursue a feigned flight, and do not swallow the bait that he puts out. A list of refusals of this kind is the sign of a mind that wants to win, and not merely to fight.

When you surround an army, Sun Tzu says, leave an outlet free, and do not press a desperate foe too hard. An enemy who has no way out will fight with the courage of despair, and the cost of beating him will be greater than the cost of letting him go. The way of escape, even a narrow one, lowers the price of victory for the side that offers it, and this is the art of warfare.

The eighth chapter, on variation in tactics, begins with a set of short rules for different kinds of ground. In difficult country a general should not camp, where several roads meet he should join hands with his allies, and in a lonely and dangerous place he should not linger. In a hemmed-in position he must use stratagem, and in a desperate one he must fight.

There are roads, Sun Tzu says, which must not be followed, armies which must not be attacked and towns which must not be besieged. There are positions which are not worth contesting, and there are commands from the sovereign which, in the heat of events, ought not to be obeyed. The general who knows these exceptions understands war, and the one who knows only the rules does not.

The general who thoroughly understands the advantages of varying his methods, Sun Tzu says, knows how to handle his troops. The one who does not, even though he is well acquainted with the shape of the country, will not be able to turn his knowledge to practical account. Facts are of little use to a person who cannot adapt them, and a map is only a piece of paper until a mind is brought to it.

In planning, Sun Tzu says, the wise commander always blends considerations of advantage with considerations of disadvantage, and so keeps his thinking balanced. When he sees danger inside an opportunity, he can prepare to meet it, and when he sees an opportunity inside a difficulty, he can find a way out. Optimism and caution, used together, protect the plan from the particular weakness of each, which is why neither should ever be used alone.

Hostile chiefs can be reduced to submission, Sun Tzu says, by inflicting damage on them, by causing them constant trouble and by keeping them occupied. They can also be made to hurry wherever we wish by holding out attractive offers, since a ruler who is always busy has no time to plan. The strategy works by turning the energy and attention of the enemy against himself.

The art of war teaches us, Sun Tzu says, to rely not on the likelihood of the enemy's not coming, but on our own readiness to receive him. We must not rely on the chance of his not attacking, but rather on the fact that we have made our position unassailable. Hope is not a strategy, as modern people say, and a plan that depends on the enemy's kindness is hardly a plan at all.

Sun Tzu lists five dangerous faults in a commander, the first of which is recklessness, which leads to destruction. The second is cowardice, which leads to capture, because a general who wants only to save himself will be taken by one who is ready to take risks. The two faults are opposites, and a good leader avoids both by keeping his head.

The remaining three faults are a hasty temper, which can be provoked by insults, and a delicacy of honour, which is sensitive to shame. The last is an excessive concern for his men, which exposes the general to worry and trouble, since an enemy who understands his kindness can use it against him. Each of these is a virtue taken too far, and each is a door that the clever enemy will try to open.

These five faults, Sun Tzu says, are the sins of the general and the ruin of the conduct of war. When an army is overthrown and its leader slain, the cause will surely be found among these five dangerous faults, and so they should be a subject of meditation. The general who studies his enemy will therefore also study himself, and he will look hardest at his own weak points.

Taken together, the lessons of this chapter say that a rule is a tool and not a master, and that the same step may be wise on one road and foolish on another. The general who knows only the rules can be defeated by an enemy who has found the exception, while the general who knows the exceptions can take the usual advice or leave it as the moment demands. Flexibility, then, is the quiet thread that runs through nearly everything that Sun Tzu teaches.

The ninth chapter, on the army on the march, begins with practical advice for passing through mountains: keep close to the valleys, camp on high ground that faces the sun, and do not climb heights in order to fight. An army that holds the high ground can see far and fight downhill, and it has the sun on its side as well. A camp, in other words, is a decision about where to be when the trouble comes.

When you have crossed a river, Sun Tzu says, you should move well away from it, so that you are not caught with the water behind you. When an invading enemy is crossing a river, you should not meet him in midstream, since it is better to let half of his army get across and then strike. At that moment his force is split by the water, and each half is too weak to help the other.

Do not move upstream to meet the enemy, Sun Tzu advises, and if you are anxious to fight, do not go near a river that he must cross. Moor your boats higher up than his and facing the sun, so that the current and the light are both in your favour. A river can be a wall or a trap, and the commander who understands it uses it to protect himself and to expose the enemy.

In passing through salt marshes, Sun Tzu says, the army's only concern should be to get over them quickly, without delay or ceremony. If forced to fight in such a place, it must keep near to water and grass and place its back against a clump of trees. A marsh gives nothing to anyone, and the sensible commander lingers in it no longer than he must.

In dry and level country, Sun Tzu says, one should take up a position where the army can manoeuvre easily, with rising ground on the right and in the rear. In this way the danger is in front of the army and safety lies behind it, which is the arrangement that any careful person would prefer. A good position is one that costs the army nothing in comfort and gives it everything in safety.

These four useful branches of military knowledge, Sun Tzu says, were what enabled the Yellow Emperor to vanquish four rival sovereigns. The Yellow Emperor is a legendary figure of the earliest Chinese tradition, so the claim is meant as a way of showing how old and how important the lessons are. A book that cites an ancient hero was telling its readers that it was handing down something tested by time.

All armies prefer high ground to low and sunny places to dark, Sun Tzu observes, and the reason is a practical one. If the commander is careful of his men and camps them on hard and dry ground, the army will be free from disease of every kind, and this, he says, will spell victory. The good general knows that a healthy soldier is worth two clever ones, and that health is a part of strategy.

When you come to a hill or an embankment, Sun Tzu says, occupy the sunny side with the slope on your right and behind you. In this manner, he points out, you will at once act for the benefit of your soldiers and make use of the natural advantages of the ground. A leader who takes care of his men and the land together is making two gains with a single decision.

When heavy rains upstream have swollen a river that you wish to ford, and the water is flecked with foam, Sun Tzu says that you must wait until it subsides. The advice is humble but wise, for a river that looks calm at the edge can be deadly in the middle, and an army lost to the water is lost to no purpose. Patience, he implies, is often the cheapest piece of equipment an army can carry.

Country with steep cliffs and torrents between them, with deep natural hollows, tangled thickets and swamps, should be left behind as quickly as possible, Sun Tzu says, and never approached. While we keep away from such places, we should lead the enemy toward them, so that we have them in front and he has them at his back. The worst ground, in other words, is best used as a trap for the other side.

If there are hills near the camp, Sun Tzu says, or ponds ringed with tall grass, or hollows filled with reeds, or woods with thick undergrowth, they must be carefully searched. These are the places where men lie in ambush and where spies are likely to be hiding. The sensible commander looks for danger in the quiet corners, and not only in the open ground in front of him.

When the enemy is close at hand and yet remains quiet, Sun Tzu says, he is relying on the natural strength of his position. When he keeps his distance and tries to provoke a battle, he is anxious for the other side to advance, and the reason is probably that he has chosen the ground. The silence of an enemy can be as informative as his shouting, if the observer is patient enough to listen to it.

Movement among the trees of a forest, Sun Tzu says, shows that the enemy is coming forward, perhaps cutting a path through the undergrowth. The appearance of many screens in the middle of thick grass is a trick to make the observer suspicious, and the wise commander is not fooled by shapes that are put out to be seen. In both cases the lesson is to look carefully at what has changed in the scene.

The rising of birds in flight, Sun Tzu says, is a sign that an ambush has been laid in the place that they have left. Startled animals running from cover are a sign that a sudden attack is coming, since wild creatures react sooner than men do to anything that moves in the woods. The careful observer, in other words, learns to read the whole world as a set of quiet messages.

Dust, Sun Tzu says, tells a great deal to the one who can read it: a high column, sharp at the top, shows that chariots are advancing, while a low and spreading cloud shows that infantry is on the march. Dust in separate columns suggests that men are gathering firewood, and a few clouds moving to and fro mean that a camp is being pitched. All of this can be learned without a single word from the enemy himself.

Humble words and increased preparations, Sun Tzu says, are signs that the enemy is about to advance, and violent language with a show of driving forward is a sign that he will retreat. The words and the deeds of an enemy are two separate messages, and the one to trust is usually the deed. A person who says one thing and prepares another is telling you the truth in the only language that cannot lie.

When the light chariots come out first and take up positions on the wings, Sun Tzu says, the enemy is forming for battle. Peace proposals that are not backed by a sworn agreement, on the other hand, indicate a plot, because a ruler who really wants peace is willing to bind himself to it. The careful commander is always more interested in what the enemy has done than in what he has promised.

Soldiers who stand leaning on their spears, Sun Tzu says, are faint from want of food, and if the men who are sent to draw water begin by drinking themselves, the army is suffering from thirst. Birds gathering on a spot show that it is empty, and noise in the night betrays nervousness in the camp. A tired army tells its story in small things, and the scout who sees them can read it like a letter.

There is no benefit in attacking merely by weight of numbers, Sun Tzu says, for it is enough to concentrate the available strength, to keep a close watch on the enemy and to gather reinforcements. The general who exercises no forethought and makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them. A large army, in other words, is only a large target if it is led without thought.

If soldiers are punished before they have grown attached to their leader, Sun Tzu says, they will not prove submissive, and if they are not submissive, they will be of little use. If, however, the men have become attached to the commander and discipline is still enforced, they will be victorious. Care and firmness, used together, win the trust that makes obedience a pleasure and not a burden.

The tenth chapter, on terrain, names six kinds of ground, the first of which is accessible ground, which both sides can reach with ease. Here the one who gets there first and takes the high and sunny places, with a safe line for his supplies, will fight with every advantage. On ground like this the quicker side usually wins, and the slower side is already behind.

Entangling ground, Sun Tzu says, is easy to enter and hard to leave, and a commander who goes in without a certain victory may never come back. Temporising ground is that on which neither side gains by making the first move, and here the wise general pretends to retreat in order to draw the enemy out, and then strikes him. In each case the skill lies in knowing when to wait and when to act.

With regard to narrow passes, Sun Tzu says, if you can occupy them first, let them be strongly garrisoned and await the arrival of the enemy. If the enemy has occupied them first, do not go after him if the pass is fully garrisoned, but only if it is weakly held. A narrow place favours the defender so strongly that the side that gets there first has almost won.

On precipitous heights, Sun Tzu says, if you are beforehand with your opponent, you should occupy the raised and sunny spots and there wait for him to come up. If the enemy has taken them first, do not follow him, but retreat and try to entice him away. When the enemy is far off and equal in strength, it is hard to provoke a battle, and to try to do so is to put yourself at a disadvantage.

The natural formation of the country, Sun Tzu says, is the soldier's best ally, but the power of estimating the enemy and of shrewdly calculating difficulties, dangers and distances is the true test of a great general. He who knows these things and puts his knowledge into practice will win his battles, and he who does not will surely lose them. The land supplies the opportunity, but only the mind can make use of it.

Sun Tzu next lists six kinds of calamity that may overtake an army, which he names as flight, insubordination, collapse, ruin, disorganisation and rout. None of these, he says, arises from natural causes, since all of them come from faults in the general. It is a stern lesson, because it means that a leader cannot blame the weather or the ground when his own mistakes are the true cause.

Flight, Sun Tzu says, is what happens when a force sets itself against another ten times larger, while insubordination follows when the common soldiers are strong and their officers are weak. Collapse comes when the officers are strong and the soldiers are weak, so that the army cannot carry out what its leaders ask. In each case something is out of balance, and the commander's task is to find it before the enemy does.

Ruin, Sun Tzu says, follows when angry and resentful officers rush into battle on their own account without waiting for orders. Disorganisation comes when the general is weak and his commands are unclear, so that no one knows his duty, and rout is the fate of the army sent weak against strong because the general failed to estimate the enemy's strength. All three are failures of leadership that began long before the first soldier ran.

The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, Sun Tzu says, whose only thought is to protect his country and to serve his sovereign well, is the jewel of the kingdom. Such a man will fight when victory is certain even if the ruler forbids it, and he will refuse to fight when victory is not certain even if the ruler commands it. His loyalty is to the result and not to the applause, and this is the rarest kind of loyalty.

Regard your soldiers as your children, says Sun Tzu, and they will follow you into the deepest valleys, and look on them as your own beloved sons and they will stand by you even to death. Yet if you are kind but cannot make your authority felt, they become like spoiled children, who are of no use for any practical purpose. The chapter closes with a repeated lesson: know the enemy, know yourself, and know heaven and earth, and your victory will be complete.

The eleventh chapter, on the nine situations, lists nine kinds of ground, and the first is dispersive ground, where a chieftain is fighting in his own territory. Here the soldiers are close to their homes and families, and the temptation to slip away is strong, so Sun Tzu advises against fighting there if it can be avoided. A man who is near his own front door finds it very hard to believe that anything is worth dying for.

Facile ground, in Sun Tzu's list, is the kind where an army has entered hostile territory but only a short distance, and the advice is to keep moving and not to halt. Contentious ground is a place whose possession brings great advantage to either side, and if the enemy holds it first, one should not attack him there. If the enemy has not yet reached it, you must hurry up and get there first.

Open ground, Sun Tzu says, is where both sides may move about freely, and here a commander should not try to block the enemy but should keep his own army together. Where highways intersect and many states meet, he should seek the friendship of his neighbours and make allies, as a traveller at a crossroads is wise to ask the way. Different ground calls for different habits, and a leader who treats them all alike has not understood his task.

Serious ground is where an army has penetrated deep into hostile country and left many fortified towns behind it, and there Sun Tzu advises it to gather supplies from the land. Difficult ground is a country of mountain forests, steep slopes and marshes, and in such a place the only sensible thing is to keep pushing on. These two kinds of ground are ones in which an army must rely on itself, since nobody will come to its aid.

Hemmed-in ground has a narrow entrance and a winding way out, so that a small enemy force can strike a larger one, and there Sun Tzu advises the use of stratagem. Desperate ground is that on which the army can survive only if it fights without delay, and here the commander must fight and not hesitate. The ninth ground ends the list, and it is also the one that tells the most about the human spirit.

Those who were skilled in war in the old days, Sun Tzu says, knew how to drive a wedge between the front and rear of the enemy, and to stop his large and small divisions from helping one another. They also prevented the good troops from rescuing the bad, and the officers from gathering their men. The aim was always to turn the enemy's single strong body into many weak ones.

If you are asked how to deal with a great host of the enemy in orderly array, Sun Tzu says, the reply is that you begin by seizing something which your opponent holds dear. Then the enemy will be amenable to your will, because he must now think about what he might lose. The strength of a rival lies not only in his numbers but in the things that he cannot bear to lose.

Rapidity is the essence of war, Sun Tzu says, and so the skilful commander takes advantage of the enemy's unreadiness, makes his way by unexpected routes and attacks unguarded spots. An army that moves faster than the enemy can think does not give him time to prepare, and an enemy who cannot prepare is already half beaten. The opponent's slowness is therefore as much a weapon as one's own speed, and perhaps a greater one.

The further an army penetrates into hostile country, Sun Tzu says, the greater is its solidarity, for the soldiers know that there is no way home, and the defenders will not be able to prevail against it. Such an army should make forays into rich country to supply itself with food and should take good care of its men without overworking them. It should concentrate its strength and save its energy, and it should keep moving, so that the enemy can never learn what it is going to do.

Keep your army continually on the move, Sun Tzu advises, and devise plans that cannot be fathomed, for an army that never stops gives the enemy no time to think. These habits work together with the ones before, so that the army is fast, well fed and unseen. They also prepare the way for the most daring idea in the chapter, which is that desperate men are the best fighters.

Throw soldiers into a position from which there is no escape, Sun Tzu says, and they will prefer death to flight, and if they are willing to face death, there is nothing that they cannot achieve. Officers and men alike will put forth their utmost strength, because the only road left to them leads forward. The idea is a hard one, and it is best understood as a statement about human nature and not as an order to be copied.

Soldiers in desperate straits, Sun Tzu says, lose the sense of fear, and if there is no place of refuge, they will stand firm. If they are deep in hostile country, they will show a stubborn front, and if there is no help for it, they will fight hard. Courage in this case is not a gift but a choice that circumstances have made for them.

Without being marshalled, such an army will be constantly on the alert, and without being asked, it will do the commander's will. It is faithful without restrictions and trustworthy without orders, Sun Tzu says, and for this reason the taking of omens should be prohibited and superstitious doubts done away with. Then, until death itself comes, no calamity need be feared, because the army has stopped looking for excuses.

If our soldiers are not overburdened with money, Sun Tzu says, it is not because they dislike riches, and if their lives are not long, it is not because they dislike long life. On the day that they are ordered out to battle, they may weep, but once they are cornered, they will show the courage of the greatest heroes. His point is a gentle one, which is that brave soldiers are not men without feelings but men who have learned to act in spite of them.

The skilful tactician, Sun Tzu says, may be compared to the shuairan, a snake found in a famous mountain of China, which answers every attack in an instant. Strike at its head and it will attack with its tail, strike at its tail and it will attack with its head, and strike at its middle and both head and tail will strike back. This is the picture of an army whose parts help one another so quickly that no blow lands alone.

Can an army be made to imitate the snake, Sun Tzu asks, and he answers that it can, for the men of Wu and the men of Yue are enemies. If they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other's help just as the left hand helps the right. A shared danger, in other words, can turn the bitterest rivals into partners, and a leader may use that truth to bind his army together.

It is not enough, Sun Tzu says, to put one's trust in the tethering of horses and the burying of chariot wheels, since these are measures that stop movement but not fear. The principle for managing an army is to set up one standard of courage that all must reach, and then to use the ground to get the most from both the strong and the weak. The skill is to make an army of one mind from soldiers of many different kinds.

The skilful general conducts his army, Sun Tzu says, just as though he were leading a single man by the hand, whether the man likes it or not. It is the business of a general to be quiet and thus ensure secrecy, and to be upright and just and thus maintain order. He must also be able to keep his officers and men in ignorance of his plans, so that no word of them can reach the enemy.

At the critical moment, Sun Tzu says, the leader of an army acts like one who has climbed up a height and then kicks away the ladder behind him. He carries his men deep into hostile territory before showing his hand, burns his boats and breaks his cooking pots, and drives them about like a shepherd with a flock, so that none of them knows where he is going. The method is harsh, and it is best read as a picture of the kind of commitment that leaves no room for second thoughts.

At first, Sun Tzu says, one should show the coyness of a maiden until the enemy lets his guard down, and then one should copy the speed of a running hare, so that he cannot resist. The chapter thus ends with a picture of the best fighter as one who shows gentleness until the moment of action and then moves like lightning. Quietness and speed are not opposites, but the two halves of one single skill.

The twelfth chapter, on the attack by fire, lists five ways in which fire may be used against an enemy: the first is to burn his soldiers in their camp. The second is to burn his stores of food, the third is to burn his baggage trains, the fourth is to burn his arsenals and magazines, and the fifth is to hurl fire down among his men. Fire in this chapter is a tool of the commander, and its use is a matter of calculation as much as of daring.

To carry out an attack, Sun Tzu says, we must have the means available, and the material for raising fire should always be kept in readiness. A fire plan that depends on the last-minute search for fuel is no plan at all, since the moment of opportunity usually lasts only a short time. As in so many other matters, the work done before the event is what decides it.

There is a proper season for making attacks with fire, Sun Tzu says, and that season is when the weather is very dry. There are also special days for starting a fire, which are those when the moon is in certain groups of stars named in Chinese star-lore, because these four are all days of rising wind. The belief about the stars belongs to the old calendar, but the wisdom behind it is that fire needs wind.

In attacking with fire, Sun Tzu says, one must be prepared to meet five possible developments, and the first is that when fire breaks out inside the enemy's camp, we should at once respond with an attack from outside. If the soldiers inside remain quiet, however, we should bide our time and not attack, because a calm enemy may have a plan of his own. The point is to follow the fire with action, but only when the enemy is truly thrown into confusion.

When the force of the flames has reached its height, Sun Tzu says, follow it up with an attack if that is practicable, and if it is not, stay where you are. If it is possible to make an assault with fire from outside, do not wait for it to break out within, and when you start a fire, be to windward of it and do not attack from the leeward. The lesson is a simple one, since a fire that is behind you pushes the smoke and the flames toward the enemy and not toward yourself.

A wind that rises in the daytime lasts long, Sun Tzu says, but a breeze at night soon falls, and a commander who uses fire must know these habits of the wind. In every army, he adds, the five developments connected with fire must be understood, the movements of the stars calculated and a watch kept for the proper days. Knowledge of this kind turns a dangerous weapon into a controlled one, and a careless one into a danger.

Those who use fire as an aid to the attack, Sun Tzu says, show intelligence, and those who use water as an aid to the attack gain an accession of strength. By means of water an enemy may be intercepted, but, unlike fire, water cannot rob him of all his belongings. The distinction is a subtle one, and it shows that the weapons of the natural world each have a character of their own.

Unhappy is the fate of one who tries to win his battles and succeed in his attacks without cultivating the spirit of enterprise, Sun Tzu says, for the result is a waste of time and a general stagnation. The enlightened ruler therefore lays his plans well ahead, and the good general cultivates his resources, so that when the moment comes he has something to use. Success, in this view, is not a flash of luck but a slow gathering of readiness.

Move not unless you see an advantage, Sun Tzu says, use not your troops unless there is something to be gained, and fight not unless the position is critical. Each of these three rules is a form of the same plain question, which is whether the thing is worth the cost. A commander who asks it honestly and often will fight fewer battles and win more of them.

No ruler should put troops in the field merely to gratify his own spleen, Sun Tzu says, and no general should fight a battle simply out of pique. Anger may in time change to gladness and vexation to contentment, but a kingdom that has once been destroyed can never come again into being, nor can the dead ever be brought back to life. The enlightened ruler is heedful and the good general full of caution, and this is the way to keep a country at peace and an army intact.

The thirteenth chapter, on the use of spies, opens with the cost of war once again: a hundred thousand men marching a long way means a heavy loss for the people and a drain on the state. The daily cost will reach a thousand pieces of silver, and men will drop with exhaustion on the roads, while Sun Tzu says that as many as seven hundred thousand families may be kept from their work. The numbers are his own, but the point is clear, that every campaign takes its price from ordinary people.

Hostile armies may face each other for years, Sun Tzu says, striving for a victory that is decided in a single day. To remain in ignorance of the enemy's condition simply because one grudges a little silver in rewards and honours is the height of inhumanity, since it risks the lives of thousands in order to save a handful of coins. The argument is moral as well as practical, and it is one of the few places where he speaks so plainly.

The man who acts in this way, Sun Tzu says, is no leader of men, no present help to his sovereign and no master of victory. What enables the wise ruler and the good general to strike and conquer, and to achieve things beyond the reach of ordinary people, is foreknowledge. Knowing before the others know is therefore the oldest advantage in the world, and in war it is worth more than a division of soldiers.

Foreknowledge, Sun Tzu says, cannot be drawn from spirits, nor from the study of past events, nor from any calculation or measurement. Knowledge of the enemy's dispositions can only be obtained from other men, and this makes the spy a sort of living window into the enemy's mind. The practical man gets his facts from people, and not from omens or guesses.

Sun Tzu names five kinds of spies, the local ones, the inside ones, the double ones, the doomed ones and the living ones, and says that when all five are at work, no one can discover the system. He calls this the divine skill of weaving threads, and he describes it as the most precious ability that a ruler can have. A network of such agents, each knowing only a small part of the whole, is hard to unpick.

Local spies, Sun Tzu says, are the inhabitants of the enemy's district, whose daily knowledge of the roads, the fields and the gossip is something no outsider can match. Inside spies are officials of the enemy, whom a clever ruler may find a way to employ, perhaps because they have been passed over or are discontented. Both kinds work because they are already in the place where the information is.

A double spy, Sun Tzu explains, is one of the enemy's own spies who has been turned and made to work for us, while a doomed spy is one who is deliberately fed false news to pass along. Because the enemy will probably put such a man to death when the news proves false, the name given to him is a grim one. Living spies, finally, are those who return safely from the enemy's camp and bring back the news.

No relation in the whole army, Sun Tzu says, is more intimate than that with spies, none should be more liberally rewarded, and in no other business should greater secrecy be preserved. A leader who uses spies must also have a certain intuitive wisdom, and be kind and straightforward, or he will not be able to manage them. He needs a subtle mind as well, so that he can tell whether the reports he receives are true.

Be subtle, Sun Tzu urges, and use your spies for every kind of business, since a clever ruler will find a use for information at every turn. If a secret is divulged before its time, the damage is great, and the book is stern about the need to protect such things. The more valuable the news, the more carefully it must be kept, and the more carefully it must be weighed before it is believed.

It is through the information brought by the double spy, Sun Tzu says, that we are able to acquire and employ local and inside spies, and so he must be treated most generously of all. He adds that the rise of two great dynasties of old was said to be due to men who had once served the very rulers whom they helped to overthrow. These stories are very ancient and mix history with legend, but they show that Sun Tzu believed that good intelligence could change the course of an age.

With the chapter on spies, the thirteen chapters come to an end, and the reader can see the shape of the whole book. It began with a warning that war is the gravest affair of a state, and it ends with the practical lesson that careful information is the cheapest way to avoid its horrors. Between those two ends lies a single steady argument, which is that thought and preparation are worth more than force.

For centuries the book was copied by hand, first onto bamboo strips and later onto silk and paper, and each copy carried small changes with it. About eighteen hundred years ago, a famous warlord named Cao Cao wrote some of the earliest and best-known notes on the text, and many scholars after him added comments of their own. A book that attracts so many commentators is a book that people are still arguing about.

In 1972, archaeologists excavating tombs at Yinqueshan, in the east of China, found bamboo strips that carried parts of The Art of War. The tombs date from the Han dynasty, roughly two thousand years ago, and the discovery showed that the book was already well known and carefully copied in that distant age. It was a reminder that old books sometimes lie under the ground as well as on the shelves.

The book travelled across the sea to Japan, where generations of warriors read it and drew on its teaching. In the sixteenth century a famous warlord named Takeda Shingen is said to have carried banners with the saying about being swift as the wind, silent as a forest, fierce as fire and unmoving as a mountain. That image, which Sun Tzu used to describe an ideal army, thus became a sort of national emblem for a great Japanese clan.

The first translation of the book into a European language appeared in 1772, in French, and it was the work of a missionary named Jean Joseph Marie Amiot, who had lived in China. Many translations followed, in English and German and Russian and a great many other tongues, and each generation of translators chose slightly different words for Sun Tzu's short, clipped sentences. The book thus became one of the most widely read of all ancient Chinese works.

In modern times the book has found readers far beyond the army, among managers who plan a company's strategy, coaches who prepare a team, lawyers who prepare a case and students who study how to negotiate. Each of them takes from it the same few ideas about preparation, timing and understanding a rival, and applies them to a very different field. The wide use of the book is a sign that its subject is really human conflict, which is much older than war.

A word of caution is in order for anyone who meets the book through quotations on the internet, because many of the popular lines credited to Sun Tzu cannot be found in the text at all. Famous names tend to collect sayings the way a magnet collects iron filings, and a clever phrase is more likely to be copied than checked. The best way to know what Sun Tzu said is to read the book itself, which is short enough to finish in an afternoon.

The Art of War was written for a world of chariots, bows and city walls, and a modern reader should take its advice with judgement, and not as a rule for all times. It is also a more humane book than its title suggests, for it praises restraint, warns against anger, urges kind treatment of prisoners and advises leaving a beaten enemy a way out. Its real subject is how to reduce the suffering that war brings, which is why it is read by people who hope never to fight.

The deepest lesson of the book, for people who will never command an army, is that the best victory is the one that never needs a fight. In a quarrel, a negotiation or a plan, careful preparation, a clear understanding of the other side and the patience to wait for the right moment can often settle the matter before it becomes a battle. The person who does this will seldom be called a hero, but will usually be the one who gets home with the prize.

Two and a half thousand years later, The Art of War is still studied in military colleges and read by lawyers, athletes, business people and anyone who must compete or negotiate. Its central lesson is that careful thought, honest knowledge of oneself and one's rival, and patient preparation count for more than force, and that the finest victory is the one that leaves the battle unfought. Like any old book, it should be read with judgement, but its calm voice still has something useful to say to anyone who has a difficult contest ahead.
